speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-63, an act to establish the Canadian Race Relations Foundation, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
There are three report stage motions in amendment to Bill C-63, an act to establish the Canadian Race Relations Foundation, standing on the Notice Paper in the name of the hon. member for Vancouver East.

Motions Nos. 1 and 3 are in order and will be debated and voted on separately.

Motion No. 2 is out of order. It seeks to introduce provisions requiring a widespread disclosure of information and even distributing criminal sanctions against defaulters. It is well beyond the scope of this bill and the Chair cannot permit the motion to come before the House. In this regard, I will refer hon. members to Citation 778 of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition.

I will now put motion No. 1 to the House.

Motion No. 1
That Bill C-63 be amended in Clause 4 by striking out lines 29 to
33 at page 2 and substituting the following therefor:
"facilitate elimination of racism and all forms of racial discrimination throughout Canada by the development, sharing and application of knowledge and expertise in order to contribute to racial harmony in Canada by."
She said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased that at least two of the proposed amendments were accepted. I hope they will be acceptable to the government as well.
Motion No. 1 has to do with the very purpose of this Canadian Race Relations Foundation. It is something that we debated very extensively in committee. Indeed, there were many witnesses, including the Japanese Canadian Association and if I recall correctly, the Congress of Black Women were particularly adamant that in the purposes of this bill there must be specific reference to the main purpose of establishing this foundation, which is to eliminate racism in Canada and all forms of racial discrimination throughout Canada.
I know from discussion in committee and from the minister's response that this certainly was the intent, but in the present wording of the purposes and goals, it is far too wishy-washy, if I may use that expression, and refers just to the development, sharing and application of knowledge of expertise. We are very much afraid if this is not spelled out more specifically as the purpose being to eliminate racism that we will have a foundation that is largely a rather passive research institution, an academic kind of institution. That is not what people are asking for.
We have had an escalation of racism in Canada, I regret to say. We have really a very serious situation. This foundation is one of the most important steps of the government and it is a considerable investment hopefully to have a strong movement to make changes in Canada. Therefore, Motion No. 1 is an amendment to add the

December 14, 1990
Government Orders
phrase that the purpose of the institution is to "facilitate elimination of racism and all forms of racial discrimination throughout Canada-" I hope very much that the government will accept this amendment.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first like to take a moment and thank the members of the legislative committee for their very dedicated efforts. Certainly they have brought forward on behalf of the many witnesses who appeared some very constructive suggestions that I believe and know have strengthened the bill.
My own impression is that this particular motion really adds nothing further to what we already have. Indeed, trying to contribute to racial harmony in Canada already causes some new discussion and new dilemma. As far as I am concerned, I am thankful that we did hear all the witnesses, that we did work very closely together, members on all sides of this House, in strengthening the bill.
However, I do not feel that this adds anything and, therefore, cannot accept this suggestion. I heard the member say that she is very pleased with the Canadian Race Relations Foundation and would hope that that would indicate that we could see an early approval, so that we can get on and actually have the foundation in place in Toronto and begin to do the work it was intended to do.

Mr. Speaker, as a member on the committee, I thank the minister for his acknowledgement of some serious work done by committee members.
One of the elements of that serious work is reflected in this motion. Not only is it important for this Parliament to consider the principle of the bill itself but to provide the kinds of directions and purposes that give focus to the activity of the foundation.
Otherwise it will be a foundation in name only, in generic, philosophical principles that no one can dispute. However, in terms of its practicability and its ability to deliver something to Canadians, it will be absolutely worthless.
This motion addresses itself to the intention to provide some direction, to provide some purpose, and to give a sense of meaning to some of the work that must be done.
We must keep in mind that none of that is going to be of enormous weight, inasmuch as the operations of the foundation will be generally funded by a fund of $24 million. If we also keep in mind that fund managers tell us that we can draw a maximum of 5 per cent from such fund in order to maintain the fund, quite frankly we are going to be providing very little toward the elimination of discrimination and racial discrimination, unless we put in the bill something specific that gives direction both to the board of directors and to the executive director.
Unfortunately the minister has to note, even in trying to promote racial harmony and racial co-operation in this country, that there seems to be a resistance. However, this Parliament owes it to all Canadians to be much stronger than that resistance, that reaction to initiatives that are positive and worth while for all Canadians.
We support this motion. It enhances the bill and gives it that purpose which it sorely lacks.

Motion No. 3
That Bill C-63 be amended in clause 6 by striking out line 37 at
page 4 and substituting the following therefor:
"siders appropriate, subject to the approval of the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism and Citizenship of the House of Commons."
She said: Mr. Speaker, before I go into the details of this amendment, I would just like to qualify one of the comments that was made by the minister.
While I think it is extremely important, and so does my party, to have a race relations foundation, we want a race relations foundation that has real meaning and is not just something that is going to rubber stamp for the government and be a forum of political recognition or political appointments to the board and so on.

We are not supporting this race relations foundation as the government has proposed it. We have worked very hard, along with the other opposition party and along with witnesses, to try to get major changes. I am very disturbed that the minister refused Motion No. 1, which we have just been debating.
Motion No. 3 in my view is not nearly comprehensive enough to make the major change that is needed in the structure of this foundation. We tried in committee to persuade the minister, as did witnesses, that this new foundation must operate as a step detached from government. It must be a separate agency. It must be able at times to criticize government and certainly to press the government to make administrative and legislative changes that are necessary to help in the elimination of racism in Canada.
In committee we proposed that there be a more independent board, rather than a board appointed by the minister, in other words political appointees he would choose, with some consultation with groups, but groups of his choosing. We have seen that he has very strong likes and dislikes in groups that come to him about ethnocultural matters.
We have proposed that there should be an independent board and that nominees for that board should come from the whole community of ethnocultural groups and groups concerned with race relations and intercultural relations.
We asked that there be a procedure-and I think it would be an important model for other similar kinds of institutions-for these communities of organizations to put forward nominations for board members, and that the minister then take these nominations and present them to cabinet. In this way it would be far more democratic and we would ensure much greater credibility of the board of directors.
The minister refused this request in committee and he also refused to change the method of appointment of the executive director of the new foundation. It seems incredible that a board of directors of an agency, in this case the Race Relations Foundation, would not have the power to choose and hire its executive director, the senior staff person who would be carrying out its policy. That is exactly what has happened. The minister again
Government Orders
refused to change the act. Under the present act, the executive director is appointed by cabinet. He or she will not be hired by the board of directors. Again it will be a political appointment recommended by the minister and appointed by cabinet.
This is a ridiculous way for what should be an independent organization to operate. It only says to us that the minister does not want this foundation to be independent, that he wants to keep it under his control. Certainly most of the witnesses who appeared at committee objected very strongly to that.
Indeed I was speaking just last week to representatives of the National Council of Japanese Canadians who were the instigators of this foundation. It was part of the redress settlement for Japanese Canadians who suffered many injustices during World War II. They felt very strongly also that this foundation should be independent of government and therefore should have a board that is not simply a board of political appointees.
As I say, the minister turned down this request in committee. We were very serious in trying to approach this in a non-partisan way, because we really want this foundation to work in an effective way. Since he turned it down and since we cannot reintroduce that motion in the House today, Motion No. 3 is somewhat of a compromise.
We appeal again to the minister to give more credibility to this board. He may not intend to make it a vehicle for political appointments, but that is the perception that will be out there. That is the danger in the present structure.
In order to have a monitoring effect, we are proposing in Motion No. 3 that Bill C-63 be amended to state that the minister's recommendations and the proposed appointments by cabinet should be subject to the approval of the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism and Citizenship of the House of Commons. Granted, it is dominated by government members, if it ever meets, which I regret to say it has not been doing. Certainly this would give cause for it to meet. It is dominated by government members, but it would give an all-party group the power, in co-operation perhaps with community groups, to take a look at who the minister is nominating. It would give far more credibility to the nominees who are being proposed.

December 14, 1990
Government Orders
I would strongly recommend that the minister accept this proposed motion.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member of the other opposition party who can never remember my party's name. It happens to be the party that led most of the opposition to this bill. That party is the Liberal Party, and we have two questions about this motion.

The motion should address itself, in its intent, to the function of committee. In our legislative committee we tried to point out that there is a very important component of this foundation which should call into question the viability of parliamentary committees. If we are to establish a foundation with a board of directors solely responsible to the Governor General in Council and an executive director with only one source of responsibility and accountability, that is to the Governor General in Council again, it calls into question the credibility and legitimacy of all of the operations of such a foundation.
By suggesting that perhaps that accountability should also be transferred over to a standing committee of the House of Commons, we would then have access to a direct pipeline to the deliberations of this Parliament, both to sensitize Parliament and to return to the intentions with respect to that foundation.
One of the most important questions is: How do we finance some of the philosophies the minister says this foundation addresses? It might be instructive to point out to everyone here, even my colleague in the other opposition party-
The real opposition.

That which is dormant, yes, I agree.
For example, while we are applying some moneys to this foundation to the tune of $24 million, $12 million of which is coming from the Japanese Redress Foundation, we are taking away some moneys from heritage language studies. Those are activities which enhance the co-ordination, integration and harmonization of peoples in our country.
What did they do? They attacked a very viable and very effective method of creating racial and social harmony in this country, for example, one that served in the city of Toronto alone 100,000 young boys and girls. It addressed a total of 1,000 teachers on those subjects. It leveraged other activities in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and other areas around the country. They took away $16 million to do what? They will finance something such as this, at a time when all heritage language-type programs together, in total, are exactly .015 per cent of government finances or government expenditures. That is one and a half hundredths of 1 per cent. Now they are going to establish a foundation, and its board of directors and executive director will have only one source of accountability, and that is to the Governor General in Council.
Canadians need to be empowered. They need to have an understanding that their voices are heard. They need to know that the moneys they put toward the financing of this country serve their needs and their interests. We cannot do it by separating the function of the board, the executive director, from the people itself.
This motion deserves some support. We are happy to give it, even though it comes from a dormant third party.

that the bill be read the third time and passed.
He said: Mr. Speaker, today it is my privilege to begin third reading debate on Bill C-63, an act to establish the Canadian Race Relations Foundation.
This legislation articulates more than the technical workings of a government initiative. It expresses our national commitment to multiculturalism and to greater cross-cultural understanding among Canadians.
We are a people unlike any other. We inhabit an immense land, one-sixteenth of the earth's terrain. As vast and as limitless as our land is the diversity of the Canadian people. But it is not our diversity alone that makes us unique. It is our ability to recognize and even
Government Orders
welcome our different cultures and backgrounds. It is our belief that in this vast territory of ours there is enough room for everyone.
We have declared Canada to be a multicultural nation and in so doing we have helped to define the Canadian identity itself. Multiculturalism is at the heart of who we are. It represents a confident vision of ourselves and of our future together. It is a progressive force in the ongoing process of building a strong, dynamic and unified country.
That is the essential message of multiculturalism today: unity within our diversity, political unity within our cultural diversity.
The true source of our unity resides in the thoughts and beliefs of the Canadian people, in the honourable and timeless ideals that have guided our development and shaped the lives of every Canadian, past and present. It is difficult to pin down and express the values that have inspired Canadians through the generations. But they are reflected in the kind of society we have created for ourselves; our democratic way of life that encourages a plurality of views and perceptions; our judicial system where equality and justice are a promise made to every Canadian man and woman; our social system that seeks to assist the disadvantaged in our society; our belief in the free enterprise system as a means of achieving national prosperity.
These are some of the values that set us apart. They are the foundation of our hope for Canada and for our future together. All of us want a better life for our children and for our children's children. We all want to build safer communities free from social problems like family violence and drug abuse. Each of us has a vested interest in ensuring that our health care, our educational system and our economy are prepared to meet today's challenges.
The finest hope that we can have for our country is that it will support and lead the human struggle for equality; that all our citizens will have the opportunity to lead productive lives, free from the destructive forces of racism and racial discrimination.
Will that day come? We know it will not come as the result of a single initiative or one sweeping act of Parliament. It is the sum total of our actions as Canadians that will allow us to move forward and to achieve our ideals.

December 14, 1990
Government Orders
Today in this House I believe that we are making progress towards that goal. The Canadian Race Relations Foundation is a foundation for and about people. It represents a significant development in Canada's evolution as a multicultural nation.
As the legislation outlines, the foundation will promote the development, sharing and application of knowledge and expertise that will contribute to eliminating racism and all forms of racial discrimination across Canada. That is a challenging mandate, but one for which Canadians recognize the need.
The legislative committee on Bill C-63, which listened to a broad range of groups, institutions and individuals, concluded that there is widespread support for the establishment of the foundation.
I want to take this opportunity to again thank members of the legislative committee, whose efforts have brought us to where we are today. I know there are other members in this House who have contributed in a positive way to this bill. To them, I express my thanks also.
We must continue to match goodwill with action. Within Canada today there is a growing need for reliable research and new race relations resources. The race relations foundation will meet that need. The best expertise in the country will be used and developed by the foundation, along with a comprehensive information bank, accessible to all Canadians.
The foundation will be of direct benefit to people working on the front lines. It will serve community groups, policy makers, business and labour organizations, researchers, private and public institutions, as well as interested Canadians.
By using the foundation's research and services, the initiative of educators, advocates, managers and decision-makers will be more focused and effective.
It will be a valuable resource for government also, by providing informed and objective information on race relations issues.

The foundation is not intended to replace special interest community groups and organizations or to impinge on their legitimate role in defending human rights.
Although the foundation will be based in Toronto, its mandate as the Canadian Race Relations Foundation will be national in scope. The legislation provides that the foundation and its services will be open to all Canadians.

The foundation will be a sound investment in our future. As such, it must start operating with a solid funding base.
The federal government is establishing an endowment fund of $24 million. Half of that amount will be contributed on behalf of the Japanese Canadian community, in commemoration of the injustices suffered by Japanese Canadians during and after the Second World War.
The foundation will also be incorporated federally as a charitable organization, in order to enhance its fundraising potential.
The over-all responsibility of the foundation is one shared by all Canadians, to overcome racism and racial discrimination in our midst. The foundation will provide a national focus for this effort. By gathering expertise and knowledge from across the country, we will be able to share and use all existing Canadian expertise. In this way, we will be able to find creative solutions to the problem of racism.
The race relations foundation is an expression of the hope and determination of Canadians to realize a multicultural vision for this country. It is a symbol of our unity of purpose and of our shared citizenship values.
Yesterday's decision by the Supreme Court that upholds the constitutionality of the Criminal Code's anti-hate law can only serve to underline further both the importance of that vision and the work this foundation will undertake.
We know this foundation will not create magical solutions. It will not solve the problem of racism and racial discrimination in Canada, but it will contribute to our efforts to find new answers. It will be good for Canada.
Hon. members, I ask for your continued support in the passage of Bill C-63. If our work in establishing this foundation unlocks even one door, if it improves the life of even one Canadian who would have otherwise known

only discrimination, then it will surely have been worth all the effort.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to the minister with great interest. I rise on behalf of the Liberal Party to say a few words on Bill C-63.
It is veiy important that a foundation such as this be set up. We on this side are in agreement with the principle of this bill. We do, however, have certain concerns about the implementation and the ability of the foundation to function given the constraints of the bill.
Canada is a rapidly growing country. We are opening our doors to more immigration. The Minister of Employment and Immigration announced that we are almost doubling the number of immigrants we admitted in the past. We are attracting immigrants from a different source than in the past. In the 1960s and 1970s, immigrants from Europe were attracted to Canada. We are now attracting immigrants from Third World countries such as Sri Lanka, India, Pakistan and South America.
The new visible minorities coming here are more prone to abuse from mainstream every-day Canadians. It is not unusual when walking down the main streets of Canada to hear slogans and slurs aimed at these minorities, often by community members. It is very important that we reach out and teach Canadians that as we progress to the year 2000 we need to be tolerant of each other.
As we grow more tolerant of each other, we will learn to live with each other. It is very important that this foundation function, but as it will not have a free hand and will be very closely tied to the government, I have doubts about its ability to function. Yes, it is there on paper and, yes, it will function, but will it support the new immigrants? Will it enhance their everyday life? I feel the constraints imposed on this foundation might not allow it to fulfil its objective.
The problems we have are many. First, I have a problem believing that the same government which decimates the heritage language program, which was designed to promote harmony and unity within Canada by allowing Canadians to learn the languages and cultures of various homelands, and then says that it wishes to do the same thing with a foundation that is not
Government Orders
mandated to even come close to offering the same service.
As my colleague from Eglinton-Lawrence said, the heritage languages funding from this government is very minimal, yet we have a minister who says: "No more. We are going to do away with it". What is the signal it sends out to the ethnic communities of this country? Does it send a signal that it is supporting their work? Does it send a signal that yes, we want to promote race relations? No, Mr. Speaker, it sends quite the opposite. It sends a signal out that it would like them to come to Canada, it would like them to bring their different heritages, but it does not support them.
The minister was brave enough to stand up and respond to the pressure from his colleagues, the backbenchers of the Conservative Party, who are feeling pressure from some of their constituents, especially the backbenchers from the west. We can see clearly that the pressure comes from the new party, the Reform Party, whose platform is more or less based on white supremacy in Canada. So the members of the Conservative Party who are trying to hold on to their seats in the west forced the minister to take such an position, which was a great change.
Second, I believe that the level of funding for this foundation is so low as to be laughable, $24 million. That is not even a drop in the bucket. What is $24 million going to contribute to such a foundation?
I see the minister is nodding and I thank him for agreeing with me.
Look at the money the guys at Harbour-front are getting in that sweetheart deal.

There you go. My hon. colleague from Eglinton-Lawrence refers to the sweetheart deal in Harbourfront.
It is very laughable to think that $24 million is going to be entrenched in order for us to project in the year 2000, in order for us to say to the new minorities that are coming to Canada: "We are going to have harmony. We are going to have equality. We are going to be tolerant of each other".
This $24 million is so laughable, it is incredible. I see the minister nodding his head and I want to thank him for agreeing with me, but that is not enough. I would have foreseen perhaps twice or three times the amount. The government that is spending money left, right, and

Government Orders
centre so carelessly could have found it in its heart to allow a few more bucks.
It is very important that we have a budget which is operational. Its yearly operating budget will probably be less than $3 million. Out of this will come the salaries and expenses of the staff. I see the minister nodding his head. He knows what it is like to fly in a director from one coast to another. Five to ten trips a year, and the money is gone. Then there are the rents in downtown Toronto where the minister is proposing to put this foundation.
Put it in Winnipeg.

The critic from the dormant third party says to put it in Winnipeg. I would like to point out that the hotbed of ethnic relations and newcomers is mostly in Montreal and Toronto.
It will be in Toronto, which is in the central part of Canada. I want to congratulate the minister for choosing my home town. It will serve the western part of the country: Vancouver, Calgary, Saskatchewan, and Winnipeg. It will also act as a liaison to the east. Toronto is going to be the hotbed of race relations to come.
However, it is limiting because of the funds. It is a small drop in the bucket and it will not be able to function. By the time one picks up the phone to call Vancouver, with a three-hour time difference, at the peak time, the funds will be gone. When all the expenses are taken out, the money that will be left over for the program and core funding will be such a small amount as to make the entire foundation a useless shell. I find this totally unacceptable.
I see the minister nodding his head that we need more money. It is interesting that the minister is in the House and he agrees with that. I know that even as members of Parliament we have such constraints running within budget that sometimes we do have a separate office, beside the constituency office, in order to operate. Some members or some ministers might.
I also have the problem with the interference that the minister responsible would be able to cause in the running of the foundation. Clause 15(3) states that the deputy to the minister be advised of all meetings and shall be able to attend all meetings of the board. Also, Clause 5(1) of the bill states that the foundation must undertake to conduct research studies, reports and other documents that the minister requests. I question this. The minister has a department. He can do all these
things through them. Why would we tell the foundation to do extra? Is it that we want to use it for other things? Is it that we want to use it to promote the governing party? Is it that we want to use it for political hand-outs? We have seen the government clearly use foundations and hand-out contracts.
What about the Liberals?

It is interesting that the NDP talks about the Liberals. May I point out to the NDP that, in Ontario when it was just elected, Bob White flew right into the Skydome. Before you start talking about the Liberals and what the Liberals did, look in your own back yard.
These clauses give the minister a great impact on the direction taken by this organization and could lead to it becoming nothing more than a mouthpiece for government policy. It could lead to the assumption that the foundation is more of a political organization than one of a proactive association for the needs of the furtherance of race relations.
This is very important as we head into the 21st century. As we are inviting more groups of visible minorities to come to Canada, it is important that this foundation is allowed to function properly. With $24 million, it is going to be nothing but a tokenship of "we have it here, we are trying to bring everybody together". I see the minister nodding his head that he agrees with me that, first, this will not be acceptable. Second, it will not be able to work. Third, we will need more funding.
It is also interesting to note that the minister said it is a charitable organization and can also fund raise. Are we going to try to use the $3 million that we will have yearly in order to raise funds and send out letters? Or, are we going to give it a real mandate and say: "You can work. You can do what you were set out to do"? If that is the case, then we need more funds for this. We need more funds in order to make it a viable tool to bring all the races right across the country together.
There are countries where the groups within it, the same countrymen, cannot live with each other. I would like to point out that we can learn lessons from Pakistan. In Pakistan, there is an Islamic republic in which there are three different sects of Islam, two being the Sunnis and the Ahmadis. The Sunnis outlawed the Ahmadis, telling them that they are not Muslims, that they cannot
December 14, 1990

walk the streets and say greetings in the Islamic religion. If they do, they will be put in jail.
This foundation, I hope, will act as a means and a tool for those people from different lands who come over bringing hatred with them. From Sri Lanka, there are the Tamils and the Sinhalese. From Pakistan, there are the Ahmadis and the Sunnis. From many other countries there are different divisions. From India, there are the Hindus and the Sikhs. When they come here, they tend to bring their conflicts to this country.
This foundation will also have to act as a means and a vehicle for the hatreds that are brought over to be forgotten. It is very important when we come to Canada that, first and foremost, we pay allegiance to this country. Second, we must educate those people who are coming over to live in this country that we must live in harmony.
The funds that are available will not allow the foundation do that. The funds that are available for this foundation will act only as a means and a vehicle for the government of the day to put out its policies. It will act only as a vehicle for the government of the day, which today is formed by the Conservative Party, to place into position people who are supporting it. Probably, it will put as president of the foundation somebody who raised funds for the government. We saw clearly what happened in the other place.
Not another Tory hack.

My hon. colleague from Eglinton- Lawrence says: "Not another Tory hack".
We saw clearly what happened in the Senate. The Speaker of the other place was promoted and put there by the government. What did he do? He more or less closed debate. We have the GST that passed through.
I say to the minister across the way, and I hope that he takes this to heart, that all the appointments that will be made will be very neutral. I cannot tell if the minister is agreeable to carry it through or not. The government will probably appoint another Tory hack which is incredible.
Government Orders
I remember the Prime Minister saying, in 1984: "We are going to place every living, breathing Tory". We are going to have another Tory appointment to this board. We realize that the Tories did such a bad job with multiculturalism that now they are trying to come back and do a little bit of vote-buying. Well, it ain't going to work.
We have seen in the recent past a great rise in the number of racially-motivated attacks on ethnic minorities in Canada, a trend which will only increase unless the government takes seriously the impact that the large influx of new Canadians is having upon Canadian society.
We know that this proposal would act only as a shell. It will be nothing but a big bag of wind.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to debate at third reading Bill C-63, an act to establish a race relations foundation in Canada. I expect that we will finish third reading today and that this bill will, very shortly, go into law and, hopefully, the foundation will be established in the very near future.
However, as I have said many times, I truly and very sincerely regret that we did not have acceptance from the government, particularly from the minister, to strengthen this bill. We tried very hard in the spirit of non-partisanship to propose positive amendments which would have helped to strengthen this bill and, specifically, would have made it very clear at the outset that this foundation has as its major purpose the elimination of racial discrimination and racism.
I would like to thank all of the witnesses who appeared before the committee. Unfortunately, there were many, many, more who wanted to appear but we did not have agreement with government members to hear more than 10 witnesses. They were from across Canada, but there were many others. I apologize to people who would have liked to have appeared that there was not the opportunity for them to do so. We do thank them, and we thank them for their submission as well.
The establishment of a race relations foundation is a very important component of the redress settlement which was a government commitment to Canadians of Japanese origin who suffered from racial discrimination and displacement during World War II. I would like to

join today with my colleagues in paying tribute to these Canadians and to the elders who are no longer with us who suffered so much during this period in our history.
I know that most Canadians feel that this was a very disgraceful period and I commend the government for achieving redress. It helps all of us to wipe out some of the shame of the injustices that Japanese Canadians suffered. They were Canadians, many of them bom here in Canada. I pay tribute to these Canadians and particularly to the Japanese Canadian Citizens Association. By having this redress and by putting the facts into the history of Canada, our children will leam about these injustices. They will also leam that as Canadians we condemn these injustices and we put our money where our mouths are, through redress.
One of the results, of course, of the redress is the fact that half of the $24 million which is committed as capital for the foundation came from the-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It being eleven o'clock, pursuant to Standing Order 30(5), the House will now proceed to Statements by Members pursuant to Standing Order 31.

Madam Speaker, the holiday season is around the comer, and soon we will be starting a new year, full fo hope and promise.
I want to take this opportunity to wish all Canadians, my colleagues and especially my constituents, a Christmas full of peace and love. May the New Year bring you health and happiness and may you succeed in every endeavour.
During this time of family celebrations it is good to renew the bonds of friendship that the current pace of modem life prevents us from savouring as often as we would like.
I hope you will take advantage of this opportunity to get together with your relatives and friends, so that you will be able to start the new year, with fresh reserves of energy and optimism.
Personally, I shall continue to defend the interests of my constituents and to consider it a privilege to represent them here in Ottawa.
A Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year!

Madam Speaker, due to this government's lack of funding, CBC has been forced to use its dwindling resources to produce only news and information, eliminating all extra activities. Unfortunately, this includes such extra activities as telethons.
The lack of support that this government has provided to CBC has placed in jeopardy the future of the Izaak Walton Killam Hospital for Sick Children's telethon.
The IWK Hospital for Sick Children is the only paediatric hospital that serves Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. The loss of this telethon will be devastating for the service that this hospital provides to the maritimes as it raised $3.5 million last year.
This government's lack of support for CBC is having deep-reaching effects in our communities across the country. I call on the government to look into this matter to ensure that these telethons will not become another victim of this government's cutbacks.

Madam Speaker, the National Transportation Agency of Canada announced on December 5 that a refusal by Ontario Express to transport Mr. William Hoch because of his disability
December 14, 1990

constituted undue interference with his ability to travel. The complainant, a paraplegic, was denied access to the aircraft, a Jetstream 31, because he was unable to get on the plane without assistance.
In September 1990, the NTA ordered the carrier to make its airline accessible to disabled persons. In response to this order, as of November 26, 1990, Partenaire canadien agreed to drop its policy of denying access to certain disabled individuals, thus making its airline accessible to all.

Madam Speaker, events in the Persian Gulf are diverting world attention away from major famines looming in Africa.
This week the United Nations confirmed what relief and development NGOs have been saying for some time, that over 10 million people face imminent starvation in Africa. At least 5 million people face starvation in Sudan alone. The food and agricultural organizations say that a major and immediate relief effort is required to avert large-scale food shortages and human suffering in the coming months.
The FAO is calling for $1.3 million tonnes of food aid if disaster is to be avoided in the Sudan. In West Africa, countless continue to die from hunger and lack of medical attention as the result of the bloody civil war which has torn Liberia apart. Again, the UN and other agencies indicated this week that food and medicine are needed immediately if a disaster is to be avoided. These are only two of the distressed areas in Africa.
I call upon the government to take immediate steps to provide additional emergency aid to those parts of Africa where lives are in serious risk.

Madam Speaker, Focus on Inputs is an association of some 10,000 prairie farmers who seek to reduce agricultural input costs. These farmers through Focus on Inputs are contributing over $1 million of their own
funds to establish a pilot plant to determine if generic glyphosate, a herbicide, can be made economically on the prairies.
Western Economic Diversification yesterday announced a repayable contribution of $750,000 to assist Focus on Inputs with this pilot project which fits in well with the objectives of Western Economic Diversification by encouraging new production and import replacement.
If the production of generic low-cost glyphosate is feasible in western Canada and leads to a commercial scale operation there would be significant benefits to farmers and prairie agriculture through reduced input costs, increased chem fallow and soil conservation practices and better weed control.
We salute Focus on Inputs and Western Economic Diversification for getting together in partnership on this veiy important project for the betterment of western agriculture.

Madam Speaker, I wish to speak of a travesty of justice. I speak of the plight of David Milgaard who has spent the last 21 years of his life in prison for a crime he did not commit. Yet for the last two years the Department of Justice has been sitting on an application to reopen his case.
The facts are overwhelming. One of the main witnesses now admits that he had lied at the trial. Dr. Ferris, a well-known forensic pathologist, has stated: "I have no reasonable doubt that the evidence presented at the trial failed to link David Milgaard with the offence and that in fact could be reasonably considered to exclude him from being the perpetrator of the murder". Investigators have also identified the person who is most likely the true killer.
But rather than review these conclusive reports, rather than appreciate the agony and trauma of the Milgaard family, the Minister of Justice has refused to act.
I am sure the House will join me in asking the minister to reopen the case. Too many years have been wasted and a human life irreparably affected. The time to act is now.
December 14, 1990

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have here a copy of a letter dated December 6 written by the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly of Alberta and addressed to Ms. Joy Langan, MP for Mission-Coquitlam, regarding the statement made by the member for Mission-Coquitlam on December 6 which included the following:
Across the country are those who would like to deny the reality of violence against women. The Speaker of the legislature in Alberta refused to allow any remembrance of the event. He said it would not be an appropriate observation for the Legislative Assembly of Alberta.
I go on to quote:
Unfortunately this statement is not only totally untrue and misleading but also contains selective references from a memorandum of mine to a member of the Alberta Legislature for Edmonton Avonmore, Marie Laing, released without my knowledge and consent.
Ms. Langan had requested that 14 roses be placed in the Legislative Assembly of Alberta by way of remembrance. Both correspondence from Ms. Langan and the Speaker were sent to Joy Langan so that she would not in fact take any comments out of context.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member's time has expired. I apologize.

Madam Speaker, there was great rejoicing in many churches throughout the world last Sunday and perhaps particularly in many cities, towns, and villages in Canada, and certainly in the federal constituency of St. Boniface, as Sister Marguerite d'Youville was canonized by Pope John Paul II.
Let me quote a short excerpt from His Holiness' remarks on this historical event:
For the first time in history a woman of Canadian birth is inscribed among the Saints whom the church has raised to the glory of the altar.

Although we are all very proud of the fact that this brand new saint is a Canadian, we are especially proud of her accomplishments. She founded the Congregation of the Sisters of Charity, later known as the Grey Nuns.
From the outset, the Grey Nuns looked after the needs of the poor, providing shelter, food, and clothing, and cared for the sick and handicapped. This excellent work continues today in such places as St. Boniface, where the Grey Nuns are still involved in the St. Boniface Hospital which they founded.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member's time has expired. The hon. member for Vancouver East.

Madam Speaker, we applaud yesterday's decision of the Supreme Court of Canada which overturned the Alberta Court of Appeal's ruling in the Keegstra case. Canadians value freedom of speech but do not want our society poisoned by hatred and racism. The court confirmed this by deciding the Charter of Rights and Freedoms does not allow the right to promote hatred against identifiable groups of Canadians.
Some suggest that minorities may be hurt more than others by this decision, but no one has the right to promote hatred. Lawyer Doug Christie's statement that western Canadians have a different view of free speech is particularly offensive. The court decision clears the way for a similar decision in the New Brunswick Malcolm Ross case.
The Supreme Court has spoken. Now the government must demonstrate its commitment to eliminate racism by strengthening hate propaganda to prohibit distribution of racist paraphernalia by enforcing mandatory affirmative action in the Multiculturalism Act. It must provide adequate funding for the Human Rights Commission and must make the elimination of racism a primary goal of the new race relations foundation.
Madam Speaker, finally, after 50 years of discussion but inaction, Canadians are going to have a federal sales tax system that will no longer be outdated, inefficient, unfair, and unreliable.

Out with the MST and in with the GST. Why will the GST be good for Canadians? The GST will replace a tax system that is estimated to lose annually $9 billion in revenue and jobs for Canadians. The GST will stop penalizing our Canadian manufacturers, which, under the present system, have been at a competitive disadvantage in world markets as exporters and importers. The GST will be fairer than the current system because it provides refundable tax credits for low and modest-income Canadians.
The 8.7 million families and individuals earning less than $30,000 annually will benefit because they will receive a credit cheque four times a year.
By next week the first cheques will be sent to those 8.7 million families and individuals before the GST goes into effect on January 1, 1990.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry. The hon. member's time has expired.

Madam Speaker, I am here to tell you about the GST that stole Christmas. In fact, the tax man cometh.
The greatest parliamentary fraud in the history of Canada was perpetrated on the taxpayers last night. The second greatest fraud is that Canadians are going to save money as a result of this initiative.
Let's look at one specific area, the brewing industry. One would argue that since the FST is gone, we should save money in that particular area. Not only has the federal government slapped a 45 per cent increase on excise taxes, the effect of the GST on beer will mean an increase of 73 per cent in federal government revenues across this country.
In one week, I have collected 600 signatures from my riding. I can tell you that Canadians do not want a 76 per cent increase in federal taxes on beer. If that is the kind of savings that Michael Wilson is bragging about, I say to Michael Wilson and the GST, a pox on both your houses.

Madam Speaker, the federal government places a high priority on our agricultural food industry.
Since 1984 the federal government has spent $22 billion in support of the Canadian agriculture industry. As well, on November 23 Agriculture Canada tabled supplementary estimates seeking parliamentary approval for $316 million for the fiscal year 1990-91 to assist farmers hard hit by depressed commodity prices and dwindling markets.
Farmers, as well as consumers, realize that the future of the agri-food industry may rest on the success of the negotiations between the federal and provincial governments on the GRIP and NISA proposals, the long-term safety net insurance and stabilization programs. This government's record clearly demonstrates our commitment to the farming community and its future economic success
speakername: Mr. Walter Van  De Walle@St. Albert

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on behalf of all Canadians I want to thank my Liberal colleagues in the other place for fighting the good fight against the GST.
They and they alone stood in the Senate against this government, clearly out of control and out of touch with Canadians, and stood to fight on behalf of 80 per cent of Canadians who oppose the GST.
They alone fought for the protection of our parliamentary rules and traditions as the Conservatives chose to trample over the rights of parliamentarians and the laws of this country in a desperate attempt to save a dying agenda.
To the Liberal senators, we owe them a profound debt of gratitude.

Madam Speaker, now that the cruel, brutal, mean, unfair and disastrous goods and services tax is a reality, let all Canadians know that

Oral Questions
such is the case because the Conservatives introduced the legislation and the Liberal senators allowed it to become a reality.
The Liberals in the Senate had the majority and could have defeated the GST when leave was sought to introduce the GST, when the vote was taken at first reading stage, and when the vote occurred at second reading.
The Liberals also had the majority and could have defeated the GST when it was in committee during April, May, June, July, August, September, and October.
Madam Speaker, let all Canadians know that if the GST is a reality today, it is because the Conservatives forced the legislation through the House of Commons and the Liberals allowed it to pass in the Senate.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Acting Prime Minister. Last night, in a flagrant violation of parliamentary procedure, the artificial Conservative majority in the Senate forced though the GST, the most unpopular, the most unwanted tax in Canadian history.
Speaking about the GST, the President of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business said: "It is going to be extremely messy".
Given the views of so many business people, given the views of the overwhelming majority of Canadians who say they do not want this tax, I ask the government if it will take this one last chance, listen to reason, and not have the GST given Royal Assent today so that it will not be imposed on the backs of Canadians.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I told this House that at that time there were over 900,000 businesses that had registered and prepared for an implementation date on January 1.1 am glad to announce today that, as we sit here in this Chamber, we are quickly approaching the 1 million mark of registrants in the business community.
We have systems and technology in place to be able to go through and process all the forthcoming registrations. We expect between 1.2 million and 1.4 million businesses to register at the end of the day.
Revenue Canada has been preparing, at the advice of the Auditor General, for the last 18 months precisely for this period of time. As of this morning in a press conference I made it very clear that we intend not to work against members of the business community who have not yet registered, but with them by providing them with the tools, by providing them the information, by providing them the necessary assistance to make it as smooth and as easy for the change from the federal sales tax to the GST on January 1.
Therefore there is no question in our minds that the GST is to go ahead on January 1 in relatively as smooth a fashion as possible.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canadian business people and Canadians generally simply do not believe this minister and this government.
Tbday, Statistics Canada reported that the rate of inflation is 5 per cent. This government has said that its GST will add 1.3 percentage points to the rate of inflation, an increase of more than 20 per cent above the current rate.
I ask the Acting Prime Minister: Will the government assure Canadians that it will not respond to the inflation caused by its own GST by having interest rates go up? If this happens it will push the economy even further into recession than it is already.
Better still, will the government take this one last chance, listen to reason and not have the GST given Royal Assent, so it will not come into force at all? Will it take this one last opportunity to show it has the interest of Canadians at heart?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a fact that the CPI rose to 5 per sent in November. It is up from 4.8 per cent in October. If we were to exclude food and energy-and energy is the major factor-we would be at 4.2 per cent in November, virtually the same as October at 4.3 per cent. It is indeed going up and, as we have said, it is very important to contain these inflationary pressures. This is what we are trying to do. The GST, as we have agreed, will of course cause a one-time
December 14, 1990

increase of 1.25 per cent or 1.5 per cent over a period of time. The governor of the bank has indicated that in his mind this could easily be fitted in.
It is a one-time increase, but we have to maintain the discipline at the same time and make sure that these pressures go down. We have been successful. We saw the bank rate go down this week by 15 basis points, basically two points over the last four months. We are heading in the right direction.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the President of the Treasury Board speaks about a one-time increase in inflation. If this government were serious about inflation, it would agree with me when I say that this one-time increase due to the GST is one time too many and not talk about discipline, which is a hidden signal that this government wants interest rates to go up again.

Mr. Speaker, if the government will not come to its senses and prevent the GST from receiving Royal Assent today, when will the minister at least table the amendments the government is suggesting to lessen the impact of this tax? More specifically, when does he intend to lessen the impact of this tax by exempting books and periodicals?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition has covered a great deal of ground with his question. I suppose if I took the trouble to respond to every single point, hon. members would think I was taking far too long.
He says that we want interest rates to go up. That is entirely false. We want interest rates to go down. This is necessary and essential for our industry, for our economy and for all Canadians. We want interest rates to go down but we also want them to stay down. With an overly generous money supply policy, inflation might resume, and in fact today, according to the latest reports, the Consumer Price Index has gone up from 4.8 per cent to 5 per cent. So we must maintain a policy of consistently and constantly monitoring these movements.
As for the GST, the Leader of the Opposition refers only to certain aspects. In fact, he zeroed in on one particular aspect. However, the GST will also have
Oral Questions
extremely positive effects on the economy, something the opposition has never acknowledged, which includes removing the burden of a disastrous tax that has prevented our small businesses from being competitive.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
This morning in St. John's, Newfoundland, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans abdicated his responsibility for the fisheries in Canada. He ignored the Harris report and the Dunn report which called for cuts in total allowable catch to conserve and preserve fish stocks for future generations. He set a three-year quota that is too high. He ignored the total collapse of the cod stock in the gulf region. He indicated absolutely nothing would be done to stop the continued overfishing by European fleets off Canada's 200-mile limit.
I want to ask a question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in the absence of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. Given that cuts are continuing in Canada, given that thousands of fishermen and plant workers are being displaced by low catches, stocks that are absolutely shattered, why is Canada accepting the fact that the Europeans who caught 70,000 metric tonnes of fish last year, far too much fish, are announcing that they are going to catch 70,000 metric tonnes this year in the face of our conservation measures? Will the minister redirect some of his Rambo-like tendencies to the Europeans and save our fish?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we do not accept that practice by the Europeans, not at all. We are very disappointed at the recommendations of quota levels that have come from the technical committee of the community, and it is coming before commissioners of the European Community.
We are intervening with those commissioners directly to indicate to them that not only would those higher quotas recommended by the committee not be in the interests of fishing anywhere because of their effects upon depleting stocks, but neither would they be consistent with the tone of the discussions that have occurred

December 14, 1990
Oral Questions
between Canadian ministers and representatives of the European Community over the last several months.
We are making those representations now, and we hope to be able to have some success in causing the European Community to recognize that not only do they have a bilateral obligation to Canada, they have an overriding obligation to ensure that their practices do not destroy basic fish stocks which are of fundamental importance to us, and indeed of interest to them.

Madam Speaker, in the last six years thousands of fishing families have been displaced. Thousands of fishing families have had their livelihood, their homes, and their communities shattered. For six years we have heard the same buzz words: disappointed, intervening, can't understand it, nasty, naughty tone, diplomacy. For six years nothing has happened.
Whether or not the destruction of the cod stocks on the east coast of Canada is a national issue, it is a question of Canadian sovereignty and is in the national interest. Will the nation respond to preserve the fishing communities of eastern Canada and respond now?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, of course it is a national responsibility and a matter of profound national concern.
The member asked me a question as to whether it is a matter of national concern. I told him it was. He then said the answer to the specific question he asked is something he knows already. If he knows it already, why does he detain the House of Commons asking questions, the answers to which he already knows?
What are you going to do, Joe?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: With regard to what we are going to continue to do, I have just told the hon. member who is perhaps more interested in making a dramatic Rambo-like case on the floor of the House than he is in having a resolution to this problem-
Oh, oh.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have just told the him that what we are going to do is make it very clear to the commissioners of the European Community that the recommendations they have received with respect to quotas are not acceptable to Canada and are not consistent with the representations that they have given to us in meetings between Canadian ministers and commissioners of the European Community.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
Once again we have seen the inflation rate go up. Consumers are now going to be hit with a 7 per cent tax on everything from books to funerals to hamburgers, whatever Canadians are going to buy or whatever service they are going to get, because this government insisted on ramming through a tax at the worst time in our economic history caused by policies of this government.
What the government has said is that the inflation rate will go up by 1.3 per cent. The minister said that this can be fitted in. Other economists say the inflation will go up from 3 per cent to 4 per cent. What this government's economic policies have done is create over a million unemployed in this country.
When will the government bring in some economic policies that will really address this difficult situation and get Canadians back to work instead of destroying the economy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, from time to time we hear in this House very conflicting views. When we explain to the hon. Leader of the NDP that interest rates are high because there are inflationary pressures, she rushes to tell us that it is not the case. When they are there, she wants us to reverse our policy.
We are intending to maintain the course of a sound economic policy because it has worked in the past. We are the party that has provided the highest rate of growth of jobs in Canada ever. We intend to continue this road of prosperity once we have settled the problem that
December 14, 1990

arises from a transition to record growth from slower growth. We are doing that now, and I think that it is working. Interest rates are coming down, and I think this will help everybody.

Madam Speaker, I would like to speak to the minister about contradictory messages. On the one hand, the government stands day after day and says that its main goal is to fight inflation. It has to keep those interest rates high that are killing businesses, killing farmers, making it impossible for consumers to buy anything. The government says: "Our main task is to fight inflation". Today it is asking for Royal Assent on a measure to ram through the GST, which is going to add to inflation, and it expects Canadians to buy it. Canadians are not stupid, Madam Speaker. The government also said that the manufacturers' sales tax was a silent killer of jobs. It seems to me the government has put the most noisy killer of jobs in place, the trade deal and the GST.
I want to ask the government how many more jobs does Canada have to lose before this government comes to its senses?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: Madam Speaker, one of the very great qualities of the GST is precisely that it helps businesses and helps create jobs. The hon. member does not seem to understand that we have presently built into the cost of all our products in Canada a very destructive tax, the federal sales tax, which makes it so that a huge country like Canada, with a small population, which needs to export more than anybody else, is the only clumsy country that maintains this system. We are changing it to allow all of our businesses and our companies to compete, both at home and outside. This is a modem reform and this is the bill which will receive Royal sanction today.

Madam Speaker, I have a supplementary question. I presume that this is the same modem reform that has cost 165,000 Canadians their jobs since the trade deal came in.

Madam Speaker, hundreds of thousands of businesses did not register for the GST; hundreds of thousands of businesses did not buy the material they need to comply
Oral Questions
with the Bill. Business is not ready and neither is the government. The government is still working on the regulations concerning the GST.
There is confusion everywhere. My question is this: What will the government do to put an end to that confusion?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if there is any confusion anywhere, it is between the ears of the hon. member who just asked the question. I repeat what I said in answer to an earlier question, and that is that close to one million businesses have already registered and prepared.
Let me quote a Deloitte-Touche independent study done on the retail sector over a month ago. The majority of the retail sector is comprised of small businesses. According to the independent Deloitte-Touche study, 60 per cent supported the GST in the retail sector, 89 per cent understood the legislation and 82 per cent had prepared, at that time, for the implementation of the GST on January 1.
It is true that there are still between 100,000 to 300,000 businesses which have yet to register. We have an outreach program, a pro-active program, that is reaching out to those businesses in a fair, tolerant and co-operative manner. We will be working, not against those businesses but beside them, to make the system as easy, as beneficial, and as simple for them to comply with as possible.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure the hon. minister will have other occasions to answer the same question.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs and it follows along the line of questioning of my colleague, the hon. member for Humber-St. Barbe- Baie Verte, to which the minister said that we are going to do nothing more than we have done, for the last six years, and that is whining and complaining to the Europeans. When is the government going to show some guts? When is it going to impose Canadian quotas that adequately reflect conservation measures? When is it going to follow the advice of its own officials and set

December 14, 1990
Oral Questions
Canadian quotas that are meaningful, to preserve the most important resource that we have?
Second, when are we going to show some guts with the Europeans? If the minister wants to know what to do, he should answer this question: why does the minister not now unilaterally extend jurisdiction over the nose and tail of the Grand Banks, because we are the only coastal state in the world that does not have jurisdiction to the end of our continental shelf? Will the minister do that?

Madam Speaker, as you know and as my colleagues know, the minister is in the maritimes today to announce the new multi-year program which will set the levels of ground-fish that will be harvested in the region. The minister has struck-I think he is announcing it even as we speak-a balance that is responsible and proper considering the conservation needs and the economic imperatives in the region.
The minister will be back in the House on Monday to answer all of the questions on the details of the plan that he has announced.

My supplementary, Madam Speaker, is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. There is one member of cabinet who has some compassion, some knowledge and some understanding in this House.
I want to ask her this. The question is veiy clear. The Government of Canada allows Europeans to overfish the cod stocks. The Europeans are allowed to fish outside the 200-mile limit and inside the 200-mile limit. The Government of Canada refuses, on the other hand, to give native co-ops and aboriginal people on the coast of Labrador access to northern cod in spite of the fact that the minister's own industrial adjustment committee recommended that this is the only alternative to preserve the jobs in those plants. Will the minister demand of the Minister of Fisheries that he accede to the recommendation of her own industrial adjustment committee and allocate a supply of northern cod to native aboriginal co-ops on the coast of Labrador? Will she do that?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, certainly the report
from the IAS committee on the coastal problems in Labrador is something that we take very seriously in our department. We are always careful to accommodate the recommendations as far as we can.
I have been working closely with the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans on a package of measures that we hope will help people on the coast of Newfoundland and in other areas. I am always prepared to discuss with him potential solutions that are raised by the hon. member and I am certainly prepared to do so again.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice. I am hoping that she has something new to report today in the David Milgaard case. This case has been dragging on and on and on. People are frustrated, nerves are on edge. I do not know whether the minister is aware of it, but Milgaard himself is taking it very hard. He has spent many days in recent weeks in prison hospital.
Is the minister aware of this? Is she aware of the frustration? I want to know whether the Minister of Justice can give us a report today.

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Madam Speaker, no I cannot.

Madam Speaker, I am veiy disappointed. It is typical of this minister's stonewalling. I want to make it very clear to this House. This minister has said over and over that if the Milgaard family would only stop giving new information and new arguments, her department could come to a decision. She knows very well that the Milgaard family has not provided any new information, any new arguments since summer. She does not have an excuse. It is time for her to make a decision.
I want to know from this minister. Give us a commitment, give us a promise as to when she is going to face her responsibility and make a decision.

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I take my responsibilities to review cases under section 690 of the Criminal Code with great seriousness.
How many years?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member knows that I have never made the statement that he attributes to me.
You have made it many times.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
You are the minister of excuses.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member was offered the courtesy of being listened to. I would say that the hon. minister deserves the same. The hon. minister has the floor.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:

Oral Questions PENSIONS

Madam Speaker, my question is for the President of the Treasury Board.
Today, a group of former wives of armed forces personnel gave up on getting any justice out of this government. They are going to court to stop the injustice of military spouses of 30 to 35 years getting no pension at all and even being deemed to be dead, thereby denying them a pension.

PUBLIC ACCOUNTS-PRESENTATION OF EIGHTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have the honour to present the Eighth Report of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts.

The eighth report of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts is one of major historic significance to the House of Commons for it is the first time in parliamentary history, since the ruling of the Supreme Court of Canada in August 1989, that the Public Accounts Committee has considered and concluded on the denial of access to information by the government to the office of the Auditor General.
The Public Accounts Committee considers the denial of access to ministerial travel receipts by the government to the office of the Auditor General to be a most serious infringement of the rights of the Auditor General as it in effect limits the Auditor General's ability to fulfil his statutory responsibility under the Auditor General Act. Such a denial of access to information, in your committee's view, undermines and weakens the financial process by which the House of Commons can hold ministers accountable for their travel expenditures, sets a very
untimely and dangerous precedent and erodes Parliament's control of the public purse.
Madam Speaker, the Public Accounts Committee strongly supports the principle of audit as a critical function in the parliamentary accountability process. For, without audit, how can members of Parliament be assured that all expenditures by ministers are spent in accordance with parliamentary authority? Your committee, Madam Speaker, recommends that the government consider allowing the Auditor General of Canada access to ministerial travel documents to the extent that he can discharge his statutory duties by means of an authority and attest audit of the accounts of Canada under the Auditor General Act.
I want to thank all members of the Public Accounts Committee of this House for their constructive and forthright input relating to this report. Madam Speaker, your committee has requested a response in writing from the President of the Treasury Board by March 31, 1991.
