Mr. Speaker, before Question Period I was speaking about the Japanese redress and paying tribute particularly to the National Association of Japanese Canadians.
The race relations foundation, as we know, will have $24 million committed as capital for an endowment fund. I am sure it will be very short of funds, particularly for initial operation, even though there will be some startup funds transferred from the race relations directorate.
We are very concerned that these funds may be far too limited to do an effective job. New Democrats support the establishment of a race relations foundation and therefore we must support this bill even though we are
very disappointed that our amendments to strengthen the bill were not accepted.
We worked very hard on these in committee and I will not take time to repeat the details. The political rigidity of the minister is very disappointing to us and I am sure to groups across the country. The main purpose and thrust of the bill must be to eliminate racism. We do not want a passive research centre located in some ivory tower in the middle of downtown Toronto that is going to be inaccessible to native people and others across this country who are the victims of discrimination and racism.
We also feel that the foundation should be based on sound analysis. It should not just document examples and put out educational materials. It must analyse the causes of racism in order to develop and recommend positive strategies to eliminate discrimination, to change attitudes in our society, and to help create improved legislation that will ensure equal opportunities for all Canadians.
We also hope very much that the government will take steps before the foundation is established to deal with the question of redress for Chinese Canadians regarding discriminatory legislation in the past such as the Chinese head tax and the Exclusion Act. We would like to see this done before the remaining elderly survivors leave us.
We deplore the escalating racism in our society and have spoken many times against these acts. I will mention just a few: the racism in our justice system and law enforcement agencies which lead particularly to injustices against native people, and the systemic discrimination that still exists in our own Public Service exemplified by the cases of Dr. Ben-Thhir, Dr. Chander Grover and others.
Canadians were sickened last summer by the over-racist attitudes when effigies of native people were burned. We saw this on television and also saw people throwing stones at native women, children and elders.
For 200 years black people in Nova Scotia have lacked equal opportunities. In B.C. there is a chronic outcry against Asian immigrants. Racist fears are often fanned by media stereotyping.
This government inflamed racism across the country by refusing for many months to change policies to allow Sikhs who join the RCMP to wear turbans, until it was finally forced to do so as a result of the charter.
December 14, 1990

I can cite many more examples but unfortunately there is not time. There are many examples in our history and these we must not forget. I hope the foundation would document these so that school children and all other Canadians will be much less complacent and more aware of the need for positive intercultural relations and the elimination of racism.
There is no question that we need a race relations foundation, but it must be a catalyst for change. It must promote better understanding of where the problems exist. It must put pressure on the government to improve legislation such as the employment equity bill which should be mandatory. It must challenge racist attitudes and stereotypes in society and promote positive intercultural relations.
We have a number of concerns which I would like to recommend to the new board of the foundation and the staff it hires. We hope that this new board will be accountable to the community and regret that it was not structured to always ensure that.
The foundation must be accessible to users to be effective.
We oppose Toronto as a location because it is too isolated from other parts of Canada. Also because, being probably the most multicultural community in Canada, there are probably many resources there. It would be nice to have a centre in all parts of Canada including Toronto.
However, that is where it is going to be. We must recommend strongly to the foundation that it operate in a decentralized way with an outpost in the Atlantic region; in the prairies, particularly in Winnipeg so that it will have some relevance for aboriginal people; and in British Columbia where the concerns of Asian communities, in particular, are uppermost. French language services must be available, especially in Quebec.
Perhaps this kind of outreach can be done by hiring decentralized workers operating out of local facilities, but it must be done. We urge the foundation to consult all organizations concerned with racism and intercultural relations as a first step, in order to solicit their views and concerns, to determine their priorities, and to find out what they are doing.
Government Orders
We anticipate that some of the following urgent issues will require analysis in the beginning; analysis of the causes of racism and solutions that will be formulated and hopefully advocated by the foundation.
First, systemic racism and discrimination in government and public institutions, with solutions for more effective means to eliminate discrimination against visible minorities. Second we want racism and stereotyping in the media analysed, with solutions for changing attitudes and methods of reporting on the part of journalists and others to promote positive race relations.
We want discrimination in the justice system and law enforcement systems of Canada analysed, with solutions to change attitudes and practices of judges, police and even governments.
We want an analysis of organizations and movements, which we have seen on the increase in Canada, that promote hatred and racism, with solutions to curtail hate propaganda. We are pleased with yesterday's decision of the Supreme Court in regard to the Keegstra case.
Public myths and misinformation which promote discrimination regarding immigrants and immigration is another priority and requires, solutions to promote positive public education and change attitudes. I know there are many more concerns that we could list, and there will be very limited resources, as the minister himself has acknowledged, to deal with these effectively.
It is evident that one of the first priorities must be for all of us, including the government, to help to find new sources of funding to develop a computerized data base that will be essential to put out publications, and to make sure that they are serving all of Canada, not just metropolitan Toronto. I do not have anything against Toronto, but I would have loved to have seen this foundation in Vancouver, as I mentioned in committee.
The foundation must not be just a passive research centre. It must analyse the causes of racism and actively promote positive changes in governments and in our broader society. This is a very difficult thing. It is difficult to change attitudes. We must ensure that this foundation has the resources and the kind of staff and board that will really bring about changes that will allow all citizens of Canada to be treated equally and have the opportunity

December 14, 1990
Government Orders
to work and live without discrimination. This is a very tall order. We know that more funding will be needed.
However, I do not want to extend the debate too long. In the interests of getting this bill through today we are just putting up one speaker. We have expressed many views on this in the past and will continue to work in any positive way we can to support an effective foundation.
We wish the foundation every success in this most important task of changing attitudes, eliminating racism and discrimination, and promoting positive intercultural relations in Canada.
This is one of the very important tools we hope will help to make Canada a country that recognizes and treats all people equally, regardless of their race or country of origin.

Mr. Speaker, I too want to add my views with respect to this bill.
Having served on the legislative committee that deliberated the merits and demerits of the bill, I think it is appropriate for us to think for a moment about the kind of bill that we are going to put through this House.
I would like to concentrate on a couple of aspects of the bill itself. For one thing, we can accept the principle of having a race relations foundation. I do not think anybody in this House or elsewhere can be against this principle.
If we are going to be for something, we need the mechanisms, resources, accessibility and the means whereby we can at least achieve the objectives outlined in those principles. And so, what have we?
All of the witnesses before the committee said that this foundation cannot be allowed to be a passive resource centre. The only way to ensure that it would not be that would be to give the foundation, or at least its executive director-and I use the words of one of the witnesses-some sort of subpoena powers in order to ferret out information that would be appropriate for decision making.
As my colleagues have pointed out, it is absolutely useless to have a foundation that is going to gather information on race relations in one city and not in
others, especially when all we are doing is collecting a library.
The University of Toronto, like many other universities throughout the country, already has vast resources of material available for the general public. We had witnesses who came from St. John's, Newfoundland as well as from as far west as Victoria, B.C. who have the same kind of resources.
All we are doing is allocating more of the passive research type of resources for a foundation. We are not giving any powers to this foundation or to its director to ferret out information that is important for integration and that relates, for example, to employment practices both in the public sector, which is extremely important if we are going to demonstrate leadership, and in the private sector, especially among the larger employers.
If we are not going to have access to that kind of information, how in heaven's name are we going to engage in the promotion of multicultural ethic and inter-racial harmony? If we do not have the material before us that would give us the opportunity to analyze the status at which we find the various levels of Canadian society, how can we make a decision on the appropriateness of any initiatives we might begin?
Once we begin, what do we do? Where do we go? Do we have any enforcement mechanisms? Do we have any monitoring mechanisms? Do we have any means whereby we analyze what is happening on jobs for job discrimination or social integration or for what is happening in the Public Service?
Have we found the means by which this foundation is going to do its very best to succeed where other policies have failed? Let me give just one example, Mr. Speaker. Under Secretary of State, there is already $7 million in the budget. I think those were the figures that were given to us by department officials before the committee. There was $7 million last year for race relations.
That sounds like an impressive figure. It is not an indifferent figure, but the foundation's total operating budget will come from a $24 million fund, at the very best. If the real rate of return is 11 per cent per annum, we are not going to get much more than $3 million per annum. However, we will not be able to take out 11 per cent.
December 14, 1990

The very best we are going to be able to take out is about 5 per cent, so we are looking at an operating budget of just over $1 million. What in heaven's name are we going to accomplish with $1 million in terms of race relations, harmony, co-operation and integration? If we are truly serious about doing something, how do we ensure that the 40 per cent of Canadians who do not have origins which are English or French are integrated into the other two mainstreams? We have to put money where our mouth is.
We have heard a lot of good philosophy about multi-culturalism. We have heard a lot of good ideas about where we are going in this country. I notice I have awakened one of the members way off in the deep recesses of the comer and I am going to ask him a question or two concerning this debate as well, Mr. Speaker. He comes from a part of the country that, as the minister said earlier on in the day, is challenging the very principles that the minister enunciated as being germane and central to the government's philosophy or policy of multiculturalism.
If we truly believe in racial integration in a multicultural society, we might do better than we did last year in our public accounts where of the total amount of money spent on multicultural programs, running the whole gamut of heritage language, cultural programs and any other variety of recreational or social activities that do not fall under any other umbrella other than those that we would normally attribute to ethnoculturally different Canada.
How much money did we put into those activities? Well, I will tell you, Mr. Speaker. Of the total budget of Canada, a grand total of .076 per cent was spent on multiculturalism. We have a party developing in western Canada, the Reform Party. One plank of its platform is getting rid of multiculturalism because it costs too much.
What do we do as a Parliament, as a country, as a government? We stand in this House and say that we have to be sensitive to these kinds of movements and we have to respond. Then we cut the funds for multiculturalism which, as I said earlier, was .076 per cent of all money spent in Canada. It seems to be the target of all our cuts. As I said earlier on an amendment moved by a
Government Orders
colleague, heritage language receives a grand total-I was generous and gave it a grand total of $21 million last year and we have received cuts. That $21 million as a percentage of all government expenditures is a mere .015 per cent.
But when the government had to cut the deficit, where did it go? It went to heritage language programs. When we come back into this House the government has the unmitigated gall, despite the very high-flown principles enunciated by my colleague the minister opposite, to say that it is doing something for multiculturalism, doing something to bring this country together again.
The Prime Minister said in the House yesterday that we have to heal the wounds that tear this country apart. How do we do that when we do not have the resources to heal those wounds? Well, if the resources and mechanisms are not provided, the opportunity to bring people together is lost. Do we have to create a fund that comes at the expense of other programs in the same area?
Mr. Speaker, those of us who want to have a more harmonious development of peoples look with great admiration at Secretary of State policies that said we were going to spend $226 million last year for the promotion of official languages, both English and French, throughout the country. It is an admirable effort. It means that the Government of Canada is really serious about turning this into a bilingual country. Those of us who make an effort to learn a second, third, or fourth language applaud these kinds of efforts because they are backed up by dollars. If we believe in something we should get behind it, put our resources behind it. If we do not believe in it, at least shut up.
That $226 million is a substantial amount of money. About nine million Canadians who would have access to a mere $21 million, which is the figure I gave a few moments ago with respect to heritage language programs, in order to maintain a sense of dignity and self-worth while they integrate themselves into the mainstream can hardly be impressed by the government's desire to cut and then establish a race relations foundation that has the same sort of high-flown principles without the basis and resources to carry them out.

Government Orders
I did not want to elaborate too much on it because it is important for us to understand that there are no resources behind this idea. It therefore remains simply an idea, something that is empty.
On the subject of emptiness, one can get absolutely enraged as a parliamentarian when one sees what is happening in Toronto at Harbourfront, for example. I have pointed out figures that come from a government appraisal of some of the land deals that have been swapped so that the government can privatize some cultural programs and some other activities. $36.4 million is going into the hands of three developers.
We could have done so much with that government money. Those are public funds that could have been put towards either heritage language or race relations. $36.4 million. We are scrounging around for a measly $24 million to establish a fund. One does not know whether to laugh or to cry at this initiative.
I had occasion to be in Vancouver and met with groups of people who were involved in racial integration on a daily basis. They do it through language. They do it through social and recreational activities. They bring people of different origins, from different linguistic groups, religious groups, racial groups together.
I do not know how it happened but they decided to finally get up the courage to protest the cuts in heritage languages. They gave me the petitions they had gathered, petitions that have been ruled completely out of order. But for those people who come from B.C., at least I can give them an indication that there are several thousand people who objected to those cuts and who felt there was no one to hear them.
If we are going to be talking about a race relations foundation, I think we would do well if we listened for a moment to our own rhetoric. We say, here is an institution that epitimizes the best in democracy. If we understand what we mean by democracy, it means little more than empowerment.
If we empower the citizens of this country to participate in the decisions of this government and Parliament, then we have to put resources behind it. Those resources are not there. Not only that, we do not even have the regulatory mechanisms to make this a viable foundation.
All of those people from those communities who want to be a vital and vibrant part of Canada and its mainstream regret the weaknesses in this bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us for third reading Bill C-72, an act to establish the Canadian Polar Commission.
A little over a year ago, on November 24, 1989, during the Prime Minister's visit to the Soviet Union, he announced that the Canadian Polar Commission would be established. This announcement was made in recognition of the need in Canada for a more focused and integrated approach in order to maintain and improve polar knowledge.
The Prime Minister has continuously acted on his commitment to enhance Canada's role in the international forum. The establishment of the Canadian Polar Commission is a culmination of this leadership in advancing Canada's role in circumpolar and scientific affairs.
Based on a concern for the state of polar research in Canada, as well as the rapidly changing nature of polar science, two studies were commissioned by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. The first, Canada and Polar Science, a report produced by an expert study group, was released in 1987. It strongly recommended the creation of a Canadian Polar Commission. A subsequent report released in 1988, The Shield of Achilles, by Professor Thomas Symons, studied the feasibility of establishing a commission and once again recommended its creation.
It is clear that a polar community as geographically dispersed and institutionally buried as Canada's requires a co-ordinated system to provide access to information on the Arctic and better serve the Canadian public.
The decision to create a Canadian Polar Commission was the result of extensive consultations and discussions with territorial governments, aboriginal people, private enterprise, research institutes and universities. It is very important to note that it had been their continued support and active involvement that has brought us to where we are to date in the establishment of this commission.
Government Orders
I would now like to highlight some of the specific purposes the commission will pursue that have been established. The commission will monitor the state of knowledge about the polar regions in Canada and elsewhere. In response to concerns raised by the legislative committee on Bill C-72, this term "knowledge" is now specifically defined to include traditional and aboriginal knowledge.
The Canadian Polar Commission will promote development of such knowledge by co-operating with organizations, institutions, and associations, both private and public, national and international, in the determination of scientific and other priorities.
The commission will also encourage Canadian organizations, institutions, and associations, both private and public, to support the development and dissemination of polar knowledge and it will provide information about polar research and Canadian organization.
Moreover, increased access to polar knowledge will, in accordance with Canada's foreign policy, enhance Canada's international profile as a circumpolar nation by fostering international co-operation and by increasing international attention on the Canadian Arctic. It will address such issues as resource development, legal and jurisdictional questions, security concerns, and global environmental problems including the greenhouse effect, the depletion of the ozone layer, and water and airborne contaminants in northern regions.
The commission is not intended to be a funding body for basic scientific research, nor is it expected to carry out such activity. The two reports I mentioned before strongly recommended against this since Canada already has such institutions.
The creation of the Canadian Polar Commission will lead to the development of a comprehensive Canadian polar information system which will build upon and be linked to currently existing government, academic, and industrial scientific data, information and biographic systems. It will also be compatible with the international polar-related information systems.
The commission will provide support for the publication of studies on polar subjects, as well as recognize achievements and contributions in polar matters. It will initiate, sponsor, and support conferences, seminars, and

December 14, 1990
Government Orders
meetings. In this way it will give prominence to scientific research and its application in Canada's polar regions.
During these times of fiscal responsibility, funding for scientific research obviously cannot be lavish. But the commission will bring a greater focus and efficiency to the diverse and dispersed Canadian polar research community and will link research efforts more effectively.
The Canadian Polar Commission will receive core government funding of approximately $1 million annually, but it will be encouraged to seek non-government support for its endeavours through cost-recovery initiatives, such as information services or by entering into contractual agreements to study particular polar problems and/or issues. The commission can also receive additional funding through donations and bequests.
The activities of the commission will be managed by a board of directors consisting of up to 12 members, including a chair person and two vice-chairpersons. It will be appointed by the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and will serve term appointments of three years.
Persons appointed to the board of directors must have knowledge that will assist the commission in the furtherance of its purpose and membership will include northerners and will reflect the ethnic, linguistic, and regional diversities of Canada's polar region.
Amendments made by the legislative committee to clauses 13 and 14 of the bill allow the commission to establish such offices in Canada as the board considers necessary for the furtherance of the commission's purpose. Keeping in mind that the commission has a mandate to promote polar knowledge within federal ministries, national granting councils, and other national bodies, clause 14(1) stipulates that one office of the commission must be in the national capital region. To enable the commission to maintain close constant contact with the full spectrum of interests represented in the north, clause 14(2) stipulates that at least one other office must be established in a place north of 60 degrees north latitude.
Under clause 5 of the legislation, the commission can exercise powers to initiate a wide variety of activities to address its purpose.
The commission's legislative mandate will be primarily that of an advisory body. The commission will provide advice to the Canadian government at a senior level and will be responsible for periodically reviewing the needs and progress of polar research in Canada, for recommending steps to be taken by the federal government to improve the relevance and effectiveness of Canadian polar research, and for facilitating international and domestic liaison and co-operation in polar research.
It is expected that the commission will report on these matters to Parliament through the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. The commission may, however, be asked from time to time to investigate specific problems or issues in the polar regions at the request of the government.
In conclusion, I would like to thank all the members of the legislative committee who worked together to improve Bill C-72, the legislation that is before us. I know that they share with me the sense of how important this commission will be and what it can achieve.
This bill is a significant step toward enhancing Canada's future as a northern and polar country, and as a leading member of the circumpolar community of nations. It also ensures that this commission will be dynamic and responsive to northern issues as they emerge.

Mr. Speaker it is my pleasure to be able to speak to Bill C-72.1 hope that, in years to come, Bill C-72 will be a reflection of what I see the Arctic as portraying.
Bill C-72 will perhaps express itself in the eventuality of having the Arctic as a peace zone and eventually having the development of a world-class centre for excellent environmental studies in the north and perhaps even the development of a university of the north where we could specialize in such things as cold weather climate technology.
With the creation of the polar commission, we could also work in the area of winter city studies and also further the efforts to date in the whole area of traditional knowledge.
December 14, 1990

Another area that will be expressed through the efforts of a polar commission would be cultural studies in the area of languages and the arts, which is very important to the people of the north.
As the member for the Western Arctic I am pleased to speak on this long awaited bill to establish a polar commission. In my previous work as assistant deputy minister to the Government of the Northwest Territories, I attended the first meetings to explore the idea of a polar commission. I had the opportunity to share with the people who were behind the establishment of a polar commission, Dr. Fred Roots and Dr. Symons.
Having said that, there have been efforts of many who will go unnoticed in an effort to establish a polar commission. I want to take the opportunity to say that their efforts are much appreciated, specifically people like Walter Slipckenko, who is responsible for circumpolar matter especially as it relates to the Soviet Union and their exchange.
Since I have become a member of Parliament and travelled extensively across the country, I have noticed that for most Canadians the Arctic remains an enigma. I have realized that knowledge and appreciation of the range of northern policy issues is limited to a small minority of Canadian public.
Over the past 30 years the Arctic has experienced substantial changes, many brought about by activities in foreign regions, including the foreign north. All of these activities are having increasing influences in the Canadian north. For example, there are resource exploration and industrial development in foreign circumpolar regions with their attendant environment disturbances and impacts; atmospheric and oceanic pollution, including climatic change because of world-wide pollution; the depletion of marine stocks; international social, economic, and political developments including greater native participation in government; and the formation of international native organizations, such as the Inuit Circumpolar Conference, the World Council of Indigenous People, and Indigenous Survival International.
Specifically, in looking at the developments taking place, Greenland, with its Home Rule and its devolution of powers, is having an effect on what is happening in other parts of the world. In Alaska, there is the implementation of the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act,
Government Orders
the movement toward tribal sovereignty which affects native people throughout the world, the recent United States Arctic Science Policy initiatives, the International Porcupine Caribou Agreement, and the possible developments in the Arctic National Wildlife Range. In the Soviet Union, there is the offshore oil and gas development with the possibility of sales of offshore equipment, and there is air pollution occurring in a number of their large industrial centres. Of course, this air pollution is occurring all over the world.
Whether the issue is military, strategic, political-economic, environmental, or some combination of all these, new ways of thinking about the regions are required if national and international policies are to meet the gathering challenge of change.
International Arctic science co-operation extends back 100 years to the creation in 1879 of the International Polar Commission which led to the International Polar Year of 1882-83. Eleven nations, including all polar nations, sponsored 14 polar research expeditions. In 1932-33, the second International Geophysical Year was initiated, with scientific investigations in both polar regions. In 1958, the Scientific Committee on Antarctic Research was created as a scientific committee of the International Council of Scientific Union.
A series of different types of scientific activities with Arctic components have taken place which can be grouped under seven extended categories: first, large co-ordinated regional or circumpolar single programs, such as the polar segment of the International Magnetosphere study; second, Arctic components of complex and highly organized world-wide or global research programs, such as POLEX; third, scientifically focused wide-ranging programs to explore new concepts, gather data or compare phenomena such as the Arctic Ice Dynamics Joint Experiment conducted in the Beaufort Sea from 1969 to 1976; fourth, programs for collaboration by a number of researchers or agencies in one area or for taking advantage of an outstanding opportunity will benefit many others; fifth, studies that are so sophisticated and so expensive that no one country can provide the expertise or facilities so that international collaboration is essential, such as the Marginal Ice Zone Experiment and the Greenland Ice Sheet Program; sixth, programs designed to facilitate the sharing and exchange

December 14, 1990
Government Orders
of experience and knowledge or to compare the results of similar studies, such as the 1984 Canada-U.S.S.R. Arctic Science Program; seventh, programs designed to combine data or information from several sources into a common format or synthesis that can be useful to many countries, such as the Bathometric Map of the Arctic Ocean produced in the General Bathometric Chart of the Oceans series.
I would like to go on to the whole issue of bilateral agreements. The initiative to develop a co-operative ethic with our northern allies began in earnest with Lester B. Pearson when he visited the Soviet Union as Secretary of State for External Affairs in October, 1955.
The following is a sequence of main developments concerned with Arctic co-operation with the Soviet Union. I think this is a particularly interesting area to go into in that it is reflective of what is happening these days. The walls between countries are coming down, the barriers are coming down both politically and in a sense from a defence perspective. I think it is interesting that here we have in a zone, which I hope one day will be a peace zone, a nuclear-free zone, that we are developing a polar commission that will express itself in a number of activities that will bring even more freedom and sharing among circumpolar allies.
Canada, prior to the 1989 agreement, was involved in three bilateral agreements with the Soviets dealing with environmental, cultural and scientific arrangements.
First, in 1983 the agreement between the Government of Canada and the Government of Denmark for co-operation relating to the marine environment which covers ships and offshore pollution under which research and other areas is possible was established. The second is the Canada-United States Agreement on Arctic Co-operation which generally agrees to facilitate navigation by ice-breakers in Arctic waters and which provides for the sharing of research information in order to enhance the understanding of the marine environment. The third is the Protocol of Canadian-Soviet Consultation on the development of a program of scientific and technical co-operation in the Arctic and in the north which was signed in 1984 and renegotiated on February 26, 1987, and which has become known as the Canada-U.S.S.R Arctic Science Exchange Program and provides for the
development of a program of scientific and technical co-operation in the Arctic and in the north.
I would like to speak about the Canada-U.S.S.R. Arctic Science Exchange Program as I feel that it has demonstrated real northern co-operation between Canada and the Soviet Union. The Government of the Northwest Territories record of circumpolar relations dates back to the early 1970s.
At that time the head of the government, Steward Hodgson, went to Greenland and in 1971 to the Soviet Union with the former Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, Jean Chretien. Dick Hill, who founded the research lab in Inuvik and Walter Slipchen-ko, who is now Director of Circumpolar Affairs for the Government of the Northwest Territories, were also along. It was the start of what became a series of formal and informal exchanges between officials, local residents, and business people.
These exchanges have demonstrated to northerners that the people of circumpolar countries share common problems, be they social, economic, cultural, scientific or technical. On many occasions there is greater commonality or understanding between ourselves than northerners have with national central agencies in Ottawa.
This leads me to the discussion of Bill C-72 and the several points I want to review. The bill proposes that the headquarters of the Canadian Polar Commission be located in the nation's capital region and that one regional office be located north of the 60th parallel. When the Prime Minister announced the establishment of a commission last November in Moscow, he stated that one of the regional offices would be in Quebec City. I wholly support that in that I feel the headquarters should be located in the north. That was the amendment which we put forward and which was defeated. There is no reason why we should not have the polar commission located north of 60.
In a time when we have recession in full swing, in a time when we have the high overhead that we have, there is always the pull to withdraw regional offices first. What we need is a commitment to have this particular headquarters north of 60 in that it gives it the credibility that it is just not another Arctic club where the name polar is used but, in fact, it is out of its location. This was our objection and this was something about which we

were sad because the government would not agree to have the headquarters actually north of 60.
My position is that polar issues should be studied in polar regions. I am extremely concerned that this may become one more Arctic club, none of which are based in the Arctic. The people I have consulted on this matter have told me, frankly, that we must avoid the general game of the old boys club and, if there is one thing I have learned since I have come to Ottawa, it is that you really have to put forward a strong case on a regional basis to be heard.
The north has the infrastructure to house the Canadian Polar Commission. There is a science institute in both the Northwest Territories and the Yukon and, as well, both territories have Arctic colleges. There are federal agencies in both northern capitals which manage the environment, fisheries, geological surveys, energy, mines, and resources. The GNWT is responsible for forestry, housing, public works, and construction in the Arctic. There are research labs in Inuvik, Igloolik, and Iqualuit. We have a consortium of experts in the scientific community in the north who have worked there for years and have contributed. I would guess that they are some of the outstanding scientific people in Canada and they would contribute to the polar commission. They would help us build those circumpolar alliances and that would bring down the walls even more for more freedom and sharing with our circumpolar neighbours.
There are so many possibilities in having the north being the centre for the Canadian Polar Commission, in which case the National Capital Region could locate one of the regional branches. It is about time this government started to break up the central bureaucracy and spread the resources around the country. The United States has focused its northern studies out of the University of Alaska, in the northern region. The Science City of the Soviet Union is in Siberia in Nora Sabers. Its Permafrost Research Centre is in the Yakuts region which is very remote.
The directors of the commission is another issue that we took to task and on which we put forward an amendment. We wanted 50 per cent of the directors to be from north of 60 if it is going to be a polar commission, and that was defeated. I do not believe that there was any tangible reason, any viable reason, for defeating that amendment. If you have a South Ameri-
Govemment Orders
can region or a South American institution, you get predominantly South Americans on the committee because they have the expertise and the knowledge. There are northern residents with doctorate degrees in geology, geography, and communications, and many who have tremendous experience with the polar land, the environment, and the polar peoples. We wanted those people on the commission but that was defeated. We wanted to have the highest lines of reporting to the government on this one.
In addition, the bill states that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development will be responsible for the commission. Again, the people with whom I consulted agreed that there needs to be discussion on this point. Is an institute with global, external, and international responsibilities, best directed by a minister who does not participate in the inner cabinet? I believe, because of the circumpolar implications of this bill, that we need the absolute highest authority if it is to be recognized and be credible because it is going to be begging for international co-operation and recognition. We need the highest lines of authority to be expressed in whom this commission reports to.
The authority of the commission will be legitimate, depending on the budget allocated to it. If they are not the kind of allocations that are required, what you will have is a commission in name only, not in what it can actually do. We cannot depend on anything but legislative commitment, so we wanted that.
Never before has the need for Arctic co-operation been so pressing. Never before has the need to learn and to develop global solutions to Arctic problems been so great.
From an environmental perspective, to many Canadians the Arctic has always symbolized all that is good; clean water, clean air, majestic landscapes, an abundance of wildlife resources, fish stocks and a richness in underdeveloped mineral and petroleum resources.
Let me present you with a truer picture. In the early years, chicken pox, measles, the flu, and other European diseases imported to the Arctic by explorers just about decimated our northern population. Later on, it was starvation. Today, it is AIDS, Arctic contaminants, and trying to cope with the anxieties created by advanced cruise missile testing, low-level military exercise, the

December 14, 1990
Government Orders
possibility of nuclear-powered submarines and the European boycott of trapped furs, the decimation of our traditional economy of hunting and trapping.
The true north strong and free? People in the Northwest Territories would like to think so. But maybe that is not the case anymore. Maybe the polar commission gives us a small door or window of opportunity to be able to achieve these goals to which we aspire. Maybe we can be the true north strong and free, and maybe the rest of Canada can help us with that, but only if they commit the resources and the political will in expressing exactly in those amendments we put forward to have 50 per cent of the membership of the commission being residents of north of 60, to have the headquarters located in the region and to give very, very specific concern and care to the fact that we want traditional knowledge to play a huge part in the polar commission.
Let me ask a few questions, Mr. Speaker. What if levels of airborne toxic chemicals carried to the Arctic from other areas of the northern hemisphere increase to the point where contamination of the northern food chain forces our population to abandon its traditional dependence on country foods? This is one way in which people manage their budgets in an area where the cost of living is 40 per cent higher than anywhere else in Canada. When all else fails, people go back to the land and hunt and trap. They supplement their diet with country foods. You cannot do this if the food chain is contaminated with pollution.
What if a cultural lifestyle that dates back one thousand years or more is destroyed by the anti-trapping movement? It has been. The trappers of the north will tell you that this is a tough year for trappers. Canadians will know that their commitments can only be expressed in a statement that I made years ago, that fur built this country. This is how this country was created.
What if the guidance system on the cruise missile breaks down shortly after being launched over the Beaufort Sea and it crashes on Main Street, Inuvik? That is a possibility. It has happened before. Trappers have found parts of satellites with contaminated elements in them in the Arctic areas.
What if the United States is asked to test a cruise missile along a corridor originating in northern Ontario
and terminating a couple of hundred miles north of Ottawa? Would the decision to allow the tests have been the same?
What if you do not have freedom from anxieties? Is it still possible to have global peace and security? Can anyone out there relieve Arctic anxieties by explaining the probabilities, the technicalities and the scientific theories to a population that speaks eight different native languages, none of which have the appropriate word equivalences and a whole different psychology with which to deal?
There is a tendency to overlook the people who live there, to forget they have strong opinions and beliefs and an abundant capability of managing their own affairs.
The Northwest Territories is the homeland for a native majority that considers the land a sacred trust. That has been and always will be for the aboriginal people, and where any developments must take serious consideration of that reality.
Equally important, it is a place of residence for people who are determined to exercise control over their land. It is a home to people who want to decide their own political and constitutional futures rather than having them shaped by someone else in a distant national capital by other premiers and the Prime Minister at a First Ministers' Conference through such instruments as the Meech Lake Accord which definitely left us and our Yukon neighbours out of the process, even though we cover 40 per cent of the Canadian land mass.
It leads me to conclude that the time has come to make our voices heard in a manner that will prompt national and international political leadership to respond to the issue of Arctic peace and security referred to by Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev in Murmansk in October, 1987, when he proposed a conference of sub-arctic states to co-ordinate research in the Arctic, including co-operative arrangements in polar scientific, environmental and economic endeavours with Canada and other western countries.
At the same time he proposed that the Warsaw Pact and NATO begin consultations on scaling down militarization and restricting naval and air force activity in the Baltic, Greenland, Norwegian and North Seas. "Such actions", he said, "could lead to demilitarizing the top of

the world", and, as I stated before, turn the Arctic into a zone of peace.
For these reasons I support the principle of Bill C-72. I believe, however, that we need to discuss the logistics, but I want to conclude with the essence of what makes the Polar Commission so important.
Arctic nations share many common problems which require research and scientific data from other regions. Arctic research is difficult and costly, but the results are vitally important nationally, internationally, and particularly to the northern people, the native people who are the majority. Arctic science requires the financial and scientific support, not only of polar but also of non-polar nations. Environmental and social concerns have emerged as among the most important Arctic issues today. Social and political developments in the Arctic regions have altered the demand for knowledge and exchange of information.
I feel strongly that this polar commission is a step forward, not only for science but for the northern people. I am certain that our circumpolar contacts will continue to increase because of the new commission.
I want to say, for Canada and for the people of the north, I hope that the Polar Commission will be a small window of opportunity to achieve peace and freedom and to bring down all those walls that obstruct us from dealing with each other as human beings.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have an opportunity to speak on behalf of my party in support of Bill C-72, which would create the Canadian Polar Commission.
The structure of the legislation adheres rather closely to the recommendations of the previous studies which examine the feasibility of this commission, most particularly The Shield of Achilles.
One of the elements that interests me about that latter study by Dr. Symonds was that, in spite of the tendency to emphasize scientific knowledge with respect to the work of this commission, he is quite careful to point out that the breadth of knowledge that is to be treated by this commission should extend beyond the merely scientific. It should extend to include the kind of historic observations that the peoples of the north have made about the north, which give them a more powerful understanding of the north, even in scientific terms, than could be
Government Orders
provided in a brief period of time of conventional scientific study.
In that context, I want to state my admiration for the picture that was developed by the hon. member for the Western Arctic. In her speech she provided an inkling of the kind of knowledge, sensitivity, and indeed love, for the delicate character of the north that few in the rest of the country have an opportunity to share, being preoccupied, as we are, with our own regions and our own preoccupations. The hon. member comes to her knowledge by virtue of her indigenous roots and the sense of historical context from which she derives.
It is equally possible that someone can leave an area, such as that in which I live, and come very quickly to the realization that the north is important. It offers a livelihood which is in balance historically with the environment, an environment that reflects a very delicate ecology, as the hon. member has pointed out an ecology that if it is to be respected is going to require the co-operation of all who share a circumpolar presence.
My leader is one who has adopted the north, or perhaps it would be preferable to say that the north has adopted her emotionally, psychologically, and in terms of her commitment. She shares with equal strength the commitment to this bill and to the north which it expresses.
The bill represents a response to opportunity and responsibility, opportunity that has been too long delayed in its exploitation, in a country that having a true north could have, as it could have done in so many other contexts, developed its own niche in terms of scientific and other kinds of research in the development of a broad scope of knowledge in an area of the world that not many other nations have an opportunity to examine; both in terms of the achievement of pure knowledge and in terms of finding the opportunities that are available in science and technology, in environmental management and so on, that could have provided us with leadership in respect to the rest of the world.
We have then another example of what has happened in Canada for too long. That is the failure to provide the kind of thrust and momentum in scientific research generally; scientific research that on the one hand can create jobs and can create economic growth, scientific research that shall demonstrate the limits of that kind of development, scientific research that would ensure the maintenance of the balance so delicately structured in

December 14, 1990
Government Orders
the north, and knowledge that would allow us in the rest of Canada to have an opportunity to learn, so that when we think of Canada we are not thinking of a part of it but all of it.
The bill also responds to responsibility, responsibility that goes beyond our immediate opportunities and our immediate possession of a portion of the north, a responsibility that recognizes that as an ecosystem we do not govern it all, nor does anyone else, and that all who share a circumpolar existence must not compete for opportunities to exploit it at its expense, but must co-operate to enhance our knowledge of the north, to monitor the knowledge that has been created, to stimulate new science, and to ensure there is an appropriate diffusion of all the knowledge that can be gleaned from there so that all can share in it and protect that delicate, beautiful area of the world, even now threatened from great distances by even tiny amounts of pollutants that can be tolerated here but which can be so disturbing there.
By and large this is a good bill. It does what should have been done, and it does it reasonably well.
There are of course some concerns, and the member for the Western Arctic has cited those. We share in common our concern about the inevitable presumption that all that is good and has value somehow must derive from some portion of central Canada, in this case Ottawa, designated as the place of the principal office.
I cannot understand that. I cannot understand it in any other terms except the preoccupation as is too usual in this part of the nation, in this place, that if there is to be focus, if there is to be leadership, if there is supposed to be real understanding and co-ordination, that somehow it must be here.
I think it most regrettable that the government rejected amendments that would have provided the appropriate location of the principal office in the north. It is something that at least one office will be in the north. We must also be disturbed, although it was argued by the parliamentary secretary that in spite of a lack of specification there would be appropriate representation reflecting the population of the north on the board of directors. It seems to me that it would have been much more satisfying and symbolically significant if the government had accepted, as we tried to get it to accept, that a minimum of half of the board of directors should be from the north, but it ignored that.
There was the possibility of circumventing the problems of rejection of this amendment by ensuring that, as in other similar commissions and institutes, the structure of nominations to the board would have been such that all three parties would have had to approve the nominees, thus eliminating the unnecessary implication of partisan considerations and perhaps patronage in the appointments, and instead had an opportunity to ensure that there was going to be no compromise on appropriate representation on that board of directors.
That is all by the board now. We are going to have the polar commission. It is a significant step forward. It recognizes the need. It recognizes the realities that we must confront. So we cannot but join with the official opposition and the government in applauding this piece of legislation with which we will not burden too long a discussion because we want it completed today. That is our mission to say: "Let's get it done today as quickly as possible".

[Editor's Note: Member spoke in Inuktitut.\

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be speaking on this third and final debate on Bill C-72, the Canadian Polar Commission Act.
The bill before us today is a little better than the bill that was introduced last June, as a result of amendments made in the legislative committee. It is still not as good as we would like, or as it could have been, or should have been. I will touch on these defects a little later, but at first I want to elaborate on the background of the legislation.
Bill C-72 will create a corporation to be called the Canadian Polar Commission. Its purpose is to promote and disseminate information and knowledge throughout the polar regions of the world. It will monitor, encourage, and support the development of knowledge about polar regions in Canada and elsewhere. For the most part it will not conduct its own research, although it may

do some. Rather its primary function is to co-ordinate and facilitate the research activities of others in Canada.
It will help develop a comprehensive Canadian polar information system. It will foster international co-operation and attention to polar issues. It is meant to enhance Canada's international profile as a circumpolar nation.
There was a general consensus among interested parties that Canada needs a polar commission.
The need for a polar commission is due to the current lack of co-ordination among Canadian research activities on polar issues and the need to provide a focal point for these efforts. There is much research being undertaken, but it is being done by a number of very different organizations sponsored by different interests and for a variety of purposes. There is not enough sharing of information between all the players and there is not enough support being given to the polar research community.
In September, 1985, the then Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development established a working group to study the feasibility and advisability of establishing a national polar institute in Canada.
The report of this working group entitled "Canada and Polar Science" was released publicly in March of 1987. It recommended then the establishment of a Canadian polar commission.
The subsequent Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development commissioned a follow-up report on the mandate, structure, composition, accountability, activities, budget and location of such a commission. Known as The Shield of Achilles: The Report of the Canadian Polar Research Commission Study", this study was completed in May of 1988.
Both of these reports confirmed the existence of serious problems respecting polar research in Canada. Both reports identified a need for a more co-ordinated, integrated system of research, science and knowledge.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Polar Commission we are approving today has been announced at least three times over the past few years. In 1988, the government announced the establishment of the Canadian Polar Research Commission. On November 24, 1989, the Prime
Government Orders
Minister announced the establishment of this commission. The Prime Minister's press release outlined the mandate and structure of the commission and identified the location of its offices. The Prime Minister's announcement was virtually identical to the recommendations in The Shield of Achilles report.
On May 25, 1990, the Canadian Polar Commission was announced again, when Bill C-72 was tabled in the House of Commons by the current Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
After so many announcements, we are happy to see this long-awaited project finally come to fruition. We hope that it will not take so long to get the commission actually established and working.
The commission will be managed by a board of directors consisting of up to 12 members, including a chairperson and two vice-chairpersons. The directors are to be appointed by the Governor in Council under recommendation of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. They will serve term appointments of three years. Members-and I stress this-must have knowledge related to the commission's work and should reflect the ethnic, linguistic and regional diversity of Canada's polar regions.
In our view, the quality of these commissioners will be a critical factor in the credibility and the integrity of the commission. I want to make the following recommendation to the government, which we have done through amendments, but I will do so once again. At least half-and we are being generous by asking for half-and preferably a majority of the 12 commissioners should come from north of 60, and aboriginal people must be well represented.
We proposed such an amendment to the bill in committee, and it was rejected by the government members.
We are disappointed that the government did not place the location of the commission's head office in northern Canada. The original bill, as introduced in June, actually placed the head office in Ottawa, and suggested a regional office in the north.
On this side of the House we recommended the reverse. It makes no sense to have a polar commission which is meant to focus attention on the north, with a

Government Orders
head office in Ottawa. I proposed an amendment in committee to put the head office in the north, and a regional office in Ottawa. Unfortunately, the government did not accept that amendment.
Instead the government introduced its own amendment which would leave the location of the commission's offices to the discretion of the commissioners.
I can take some comfort from the fact that the government backed off the Ottawa head office location, but I regret that it would not agree to put that head office in the north. I am very pleased that the government has accepted this.
I am sure that they really had no choice but to accept it. It is the recognition of aboriginal knowledge in this bill. We were advised by the government in committee that the use of this word, in addition to the term "science" was meant to incorporate aboriginal knowledge. "The recognition was implicit," they said.
We wanted the recognition to be explicit. We wanted the recognition to be clear. I, therefore, moved an amendment in committee that defines "knowledge" to include traditional and aboriginal knowledge. That amendment was accepted by the government and passed in committee. I would like to take this opportunity to thank the members of the committee for their support.
I believe that for the first time in legislation, northern and aboriginal people now have their intimate understanding and awareness of their environment, and the wildlife recognized and affirmed.
We have had difficulties in the past with scientific and biological research. Much activity has gone on without our participation and involvement.
There have been conflicts between the traditional knowledge of aboriginal people and the scientific data bases of non-aboriginal researchers. In the second reading debate on this bill, I mentioned a past conflict over the counting of a caribou herd in the Keewatin, and an ongoing dispute over beluga whales in the Baffin region.
We hope that this polar commission will help to avoid these problems by fully involving northern and aboriginal
people in the ongoing and future research into our region.
We canvassed a great number of organizations, aboriginal and non-aboriginal, on the concept of a polar commission. All were very supportive.
Some concerns were expressed, however, concerning the mandate of the commission. It was thought, for example, that the commission should be able to advise the government at any time, and not just when requested, as the bill is currently written. In committee, I moved an amendment which would have given the commission the freedom to advise the government at any time, but that amendment was rejected by the government.
We still have some concerns about the adequacy of the commission's budget, and about its independence from the government. We regret that the government did not seem to want to hear from any witnesses on this legislation. We were told that we would risk losing this bill if we took the time to hear from interested organizations.
None of the groups we talked to wanted to take the chance of losing this bill, so we moved forward, but I still believe the committee could have benefited from the comments of those directly involved in northern issues research.
In conclusion, our members on this side of the House support this bill. It is an initiative which is long overdue.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief because I understand there is agreement on this piece of legislation. We know that there have been some technical amendments proposed in two different areas.
I want to thank the legislative committee which considered the bill and received presentations from various interests. I want to express my appreciation for the contribution of the committee which did all of this work. I also want to commend the members of the committee for their time, their input, and for their co-operation in ensuring this bill's prompt review. [Editor's note: Member spoke in Inuktitut.]

Mr. Speaker, I would like to be very brief but you must also realize that we do have some comments on this bill. I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak at third reading stage of Bill C-68.
When I spoke at second reading I indicated, on behalf of my party, the Official Opposition, my support for this bill but with some reservations. We support this bill because it corrects an oversight, a negligence of the government. We support the corrective steps in this bill which strengthen the protection of lands withdrawn in the Yukon for the purpose of lands claims settlements.
We continue to regret the negligence of the government which had the unfortunate effect of infringing on the aboriginal rights of the Yukon Indian people and, in particular, those represented by the Kluane Tribal Council. We continue to caution the government that it must take its constitutional trust responsibilities toward aboriginal peoples much more seriously.
The government initially wanted to pass this bill, in all stages, on a single day. We insisted that it should go to a legislative committee so that groups affected by the legislation would have an opportunity to express their views and recommend any changes they thought were necessary.
This was a very useful exercise, as the government will agree because, after hearing witnesses, the government brought forward amendments to its own legislation. It is interesting that the amendments introduced by the government responded to concerns expressed by the mining industry and prospectors. The government did not bring forward any amendments to respond to the concerns of the Yukon Indian people.
I would like to take a few moments to communicate to this House what the Kluane Tribal Council and the Council for Yukon Indians had to say about this bill in committee. They reminded committee members that the need for this bill arose out of a failure of a federal Order in Council which was supposed to protect a portion of the unsurrendered homelands of the Kluane Tribal Council from mineral staking. I want to describe to this House the history and background of the bill and the issues we are dealing with today.

December 14, 1990
Government Orders
For the past several years, Mr. Speaker, the government has, from time to time and for various public purposes, including the settlement of aboriginal land claims, withdrawn various parcels of land in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories from this position.
As hon. members know, all of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories are the subject of land claims negotiations with aboriginal peoples. These aboriginal people negotiating these claims have long been concerned about the alienation by third parties of lands which they are claiming while negotiations are ongoing.
The federal government has, in response to these concerns, ordered the freezing or withdrawal of certain lands designated by aboriginal claimants from disposition, pending settlement of the particular land claim under negotiation. The withdrawal of these lands has removed the possibility of third-party interest being created in such lands, at least for the duration of the withdrawal order.
Negotiations between the aboriginal people and the government determine which lands will be withdrawn. There is a general criteria which describes lands which cannot be withdrawn; such lands are lands which are already privately owned. In each land claim area there are more specific criteria used by the federal government in the decision-making, but these criteria are not public nor are they made available to the aboriginal claimants.
In the Yukon, the Council for Yukon Indians has been negotiating a land claims agreement since 1973, and in March, 1989, negotiators for the Government of Canada and the Council for Yukon Indians ratified an agreement in principle.
Several parcels of land have been withdrawn for Yukon Indians pending final settlement of their land claims. Section 23 of the Territorial Lands Act permits governments to designate and withdraw from dispositions certain parcels of land.
In addition, Section 98 of the Yukon Placer Mining Act permits the Governor in Council to prohibit entry on certain lands for the purpose of locating a claim or prospecting for gold or other precious minerals or stones. The Yukon Quartz Mining Act contains no provision to withdraw lands or prohibit mining on certain lands. However, Section 14 of the Yukon Quartz Mining
Act does provide for exceptions to the general right to acquire mineral rights.
It has been the position of the government that a withdrawal made under Section 23 of the Territorial Lands Act should be considered a reservation within the meaning of Section 14 of the Yukon Quartz Mining Act. The government's position, however, was challenged in court by an individual prospector. The prospector had staked 265 mineral claims in an area withdrawn for settlements of the Kluane Tribal Council land claims. These claims were refused by the mining recorder because they were staked on lands withdrawn for the settlement of the Indian land claims.
The prospector brought the matter to Federal Court on July 12, 1988. On February 12, 1990, a judgment in favour of the prospector was handed down. The judgment was based on the fact that subsection 3(3) of the Territorial Lands Act states that "nothing in this act shall be construed as limiting the operation of the Yukon Quartz Mining Act, the Yukon Placer Mining Act, the Dominion Water Power Act, or the National Parks Act". The judge decided therefore that any withdrawal orders made pursuant to the Territorial Lands Act could not have an effect on the Yukon Quartz Mining Act. In other words, he said that claim staking under the Yukon Quartz Mining Act could not be curtailed by orders pursuant to the Territorial Lands Act. The judge ordered that mining recorder to accept the prospector's claims.
The day after the court decision, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development announced in the House that the government would be introducing legislation to amend the Yukon Quartz Mining Act and the Yukon Placer Mining Act. He also announced that legislation would be retroactive to February 13, the date of his announcement.
On March 9, 1990, Bill C-68 was introduced. This bill amends two pieces of legislation, the Yukon Placer Mining Act and the Yukon Quartz Mining Act. It will clarify and confirm the government's right to prohibit mineral claims staking on certain lands which may be required for the settlement of aboriginal land claims by specifying this purpose in both of these acts. The changes are essentially technical changes, and as I mentioned earlier, they are retroactive to February 13, 1990.

This bill closes a loophole in the Yukon Quartz Mining Act which allowed a prospector to stake mineral claims on lands selected by the Kluane Tribal Council and withdrawn by the government for the settlement of their claim. It provides for a greater certainty in the Yukon Placer Mining Act. As such, it is an improvement on the current situation pending a final court determination.
I should point out, Mr. Speaker, that the federal government on March 7 filed an appeal on the February 12 court decision with the Federal Court of Appeals.
There are no strong objections to the remedy provided by this bill. The mining associations of the Yukon are generally concerned about the amount of land which has been withdrawn, but support the land claims settlement process and the bill because it provides for great uncertainty for the industry.
The CYI concluded, however, after reviewing Bill C-68, that it does not go far enough in terms of protection which is to be provided to the unsurrendered lands of the Kluane Tribal Council and the other Yukon first nations. Their primary recommendations to the committee was to amend Bill C-68 so as to prevent staking or mining on the unsurrendered land of the Yukon First Nations until such time as their claims to those lands have been settled, or they have otherwise expressly consented to such staking or mining.
I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that my office did try to frame an amendment between the time the committee had finished with the bill and this debate today to respond to that concern expressed by the Yukon Indians. We were told by legal counsel, however, that our amendment would be out of order because it went beyond the scope of this bill.
Unfortunately, this bill is not constructed in a way that permitted us to strengthen the position of the Yukon First Nations. We regret that, and we wish we could have done more to protect the rights of the Yukon Indians. We recognize that the bill before us at least takes a step in that direction.
In conclusion, we support this bill because it closes the loopholes the government was not aware of. It corrects a mistake caused by the government's negligence. It is an improvement on the present situation but, I stress, it
Government Orders
does not go far enough to protect the unsurrendered aboriginal lands from third-party alienation.
Aboriginal people involved in land claims negotiations continue to see their lands alienated, despite the fact that no settlement of their claim has been reached. This occurs in the Yukon, in the Northwest Territories, and in British Columbia. Revisions to the land claims policy are needed to better protect aboriginal interests, rights, and titles.

Mr. Speaker, I must say that I had a long speech to give on this Bill C-68, but my hon. friend from Nunatsiaq has laid it out for the House very thoroughly and comprehensively. I feel I now have to emphasize only two or three points that he made at the very end of his presentation.
I would like to congratulate him in terms of laying out the history of this whole issue, and also to acknowledge the fact that much was done in committee in a very co-operative way to advance the situation that existed in the Yukon. As my hon. friend from Nunatsiaq has indicated, there are still some problems with this bill.
The fact that the Kluane Tribal Council and the Council of Yukon Indians maintain that this bill does not go far enough in protecting their unsurrendered lands in their continuing negotiations over land claims, is something that we, as members, ought not to take lightly.
We are pleased in terms of the progress that it has shown, not only in terms of the land claims settlement in the Yukon, but also the progress shown in this bill. It is also important to acknowledge the fact that these outstanding issues and concerns remain.
Both the tribal council and the Council of Yukon Indians wanted Bill C-68 amended to prevent staking and mining on their unsurrendered lands until the land claims are settled, or they have given consent for this type of activity. The Council of Yukon Indians maintains that our Canadian constitution requires the land claims be settled before their homelands are opened up for use by others. I recall that a legal opinion by Tom Berger supports this claim that the Council of Yukon Indians makes.
Perhaps I can give a moment or two or background in the time remaining. When the British North America Act established the Dominion of Canada back in 1867, the Yukon First Nation land was not part of Canada.

Government Orders
Canada wanted to acquire Rupert's Land in the northwestern territory in order to extend Canada to the Arctic Ocean. The conditions, Mr. Speaker, that you probably will recall as a student of history, as well as constitutional history, set up by the Senate and the House of Commons in 1867, said the homelands transferred "-will be considered and settled in conformity with the equitable principles which have uniformly governed the British Crown in the dealings with the aborigines". Does that not sum it up, Mr. Speaker, clearly for all of us?
This was accomplished through various treaties which allotted lands for settlement by non-natives. This existed until the Klondike Gold Rush, from which time to the present, the Council of Yukon Indians says represents a breach by the government in allowing lands to be used, and if I may say abused, as well, while no attempts were made to settle claims on the unsurrendered lands. Natives claim that Canada is not honouring its constitutional duties to natives in the Yukon because unsurrendered lands are not being protected.
As well, the Council of Yukon Indians, does not wish to reverse development, just to freeze it, until land claims can be settled in order to prevent alienations in the future.
I would refer to the the claims staked by the miner, Mr. Halferdahl, in an area that was desired by the native people. The miner was able to retain these because of a loophole in the Territorial Lands Act. He took these claims to court, as my hon. colleague has already pointed out, and his position was upheld. The point is that if Bill C-68 was made retroactive to 1987, he would lose his claims and would have to be compensated according to the government. Fair enough. If he keeps his claims by virtue of Bill C-68 being effective in February 1990, will the government compensate the Council of Yukon Indians? I think this is a critical question now that we must pursue.
The Council of Yukon Indians has said that it has been involved in negotiations for compensation for many, many years while this particular miner has only been involved briefly and yet the government is prepared to offer compensation to him.
While we in the New Democratic Party support Bill C-68, let us all acknowledge that much work remains to
be done and we look forward to the appropriate committee and those interested members of the House to continue with their interest in this issue in terms of improving it even more in the future.
