He said: Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for seconding my motion to allow it to be presented.
This particular bill enables young people 16 years and over to vote in federal elections. I might say that I think all of us have had innumerable experiences as we have met young people in our careers as parliamentarians and recognized and acknowledged the fact that many young people, age 16, 17, and perhaps even a lot younger than that, are quite capable of making a judgment when it comes to who ought to represent them in the Parliament of Canada, which political party, which political persuasion if you like, the kind of person. I hope one day that we can expand this so 16-year olds will also have the opportunity perhaps to elect senators and be senators, to represent a more democratic approach to political decision-making in our country.
I want to make my case by first of all acknowledging the discussions I have had with groups of young people, particularly in a formal sense, from Cariboo University College, from Brocklehurst Secondary School, Norkam Secondary, Kam High, Westsyde Secondary, Barriere

December 14, 1990
Private Members' Business
Secondary, Clearwater Secondary, Chase Secondary, Logan Lake Secondary, as well as a whole host of junior high schools. Also, on a number of occasions with the more senior years in elementary school where we discussed what age would be appropriate in terms of people voting in general elections. After these discussions and recognizing the understanding that young people today have of international affairs and national affairs, the understanding of the legislative process, it is with no hesitation that I say that I believe it is appropriate that we change legislation to empower those youngsters who are 16 and 17 years of age to be able to vote in our general elections.
The reasons for this are many. At age 16 young people are able to join the Armed Forces of Canada. I believe if we say to a young man or young woman that at age 16 with parental consent you are able to join the Armed Forces of Canada and go off to represent Canada in perhaps, unfortunately, places of conflict, they ought also to have the right to decide on those people who will represent them in the nation's Parliament.
At age 16 young people are able to get married legally, again with parental consent, but marriage and the responsibilities of marriage surely indicate that at that age people are capable of taking on the responsibilities of very serious decision-making.
Of course, at age 16 young people are able to drive vehicles, high powered cars, and take the responsibility of driving safely and manoeuvring an automobile down our crowded highways. Surely with that responsibility, we can assume that young people have the ability to make veiy thoughtful decisions in terms of those representing them in Parliament.
We also recognize that many young people aged 16 are working full time, or part time at least, as a result of supporting themselves through their senior level of school. As a result, they are subject to the minimum wage. At age 16 the minimum wage becomes effective. Again we recognize that particular age of change in a young person's life.
We also recognize that as these young people work, they need a full time or part time job, they are contributing to the unemployment insurance plan. They are
paying their taxes if their incomes are of a particular level and contributing to society in a regular way.
I might say also that many young people take on responsibilities now that I am impressed with. I almost consider it to be awesome in terms of the way they approach their studies, the way they are involved in community groups and organizations and make contributions in very serious ways.
I have sat with friends of my sons and discussed national political issues only to be moved after hearing the extent to which these young people are aware of issues and how they are able to articulate their concerns, maturity, thoughtfulness and wisdom of the views that they hold. They are not necessarily always the same as my own.
I recognize that people view a particular item or an issue-nationally, internationally, even locally-with different biases. As a result, they have different views. But I have always been impressed with their ability to analyse.
It is fair to say that these days, as a result of the sophisticated educational programs, of the communications systems that enable young people to be instantaneously informed about issues around the globe, these young people are quite capable of deciding, if they wish, who ought to represent them in the nation's Parliament.
Some people react by saying: "These people are simply too young to make a decision. They are too inexperienced. They just do not have the background". I hate to say this, but not too many years ago people made those same claims about native people. It is almost one of our national disgraces when we think that it was only back in the 1950s when native people were permitted to vote. Again, a very dark mark on Canadian history.
If you look back at the debates of that time, people were saying: "Do native people have the information, experience and the background to make an intelligent decision?" Well, of course, they did and to even think about it and question it now would be an embarrassment.
Not too many years ago, on May 24, 1918, the decision was made to give women the vote. When you look back at those debates and those discussions, it was the same thing: "Are women able to make a serious decision?".

When we think back now, it is laughable to even think that those discussions took place.
When people scoff at or reject the idea outright that young people aged 16 and 17 are incapable of making a decision, let us remember that these same young people are capable of making decisions in terms of participating in the Armed Forces, participating as drivers on our highways, participating meaningfully in the workplace or entering into a state of matrimony.
For those reasons, Madam Speaker, I submit to you that we ought to consider changes to legislation in order to provide young people aged 16 and 17 an opportunity to vote in national elections. I can hardly pass without making the observation that, in all of the discussions I have had with young people who are interested in the state of affairs of the day, and I will acknowledge that many are not, young people do not lay awake night after night worrying about our trade with Bolivia or many of the other items that we concern ourselves with in this House, but many do. The fact is that many young people do take the issues before us and our national political agenda very seriously.
I must say that the times I have spent in discussions, either with clubs in schools or universities and informal and formal organizations across the country, these people are-and I am hesitant to say it but I think it is very true-much more informed than many people who are participating in the electoral process. I often wonder what it is that motivates people to cast ballots in certain directions. I think we probably are not as bad as the United States, but we see sort of creeping into our electoral system reasons for casting political decisions that are somewhat suspect in terms of their intellectual weight and wisdom.
However, it is time that we provide an opportunity for these young people ages 16 and 17 to vote. That is not saying that we require every person at age 16 to vote because many are not interested and perhaps do not feel an inclination to participate in the electoral process. But for those increasing numbers who do, who recognize that the decisions made in the House of Commons of Canada will have a profound effect on their lives, and I do not have to go any further than to refer to what we will do

Whether you look at the tax system as it affects young people and the educational policy of the federal government in terms of their futures, colleges, universities and technical and vocational schools, whether you consider the support or lack of support by the federal government in terms of research and development, in terms of economic development, when you look at regional development programs and whether they create more jobs or result in job loss, these are all issues that most young people are very concerned about.
Post-secondary education. When you look, Mr. Speaker, at what the government is doing in terms of post-secondary education, this is a major implication for the young people of today. When you look at fiscal policy, monetary policy, foreign policy, social policy, they all directly affect the lives of our young people. They have a very serious vested interest in the future because they are going to live the rest of their lives there. For that reason, I believe it is appropriate that all of us recognize the value of this bill. It is something that I and my party have recommended to the Royal Commission on Electoral Reform, a Royal commission that toured the country earlier this year seeking input from various groups and political parties on necessary changes, and I am proud to say that it was the federal New Democratic Party that made this recommendation that when the changes to the electoral laws are drafted, consideration be given to have age 16 as the year where Canadians would be eligible to vote in federal elections.

I look forward to the support from my colleagues in the House of Commons from the Liberal Party, as well as the Progressive Conservative Party, and look forward to the day when we provide the opportunity for young people to be empowered so that they are involved in a serious meaningful way in deciding on the next federal government of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CANADA ELECTIONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that my speech will probably be interrupted by a number of knocks on the door later on, when we are asked to- I don't want to be rude and ask the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, when he comes from the Senate, to wait a minute-we have been waiting for quite some time-nor would I want the newspapers to report tomorrow that a masterful speech by the hon. member for Beauhamois was interrupted by a member of the Senate.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, since we are talking about the right to vote, I would like to take this opportunity to pay tribute to one country in particular, Haiti, which next Sunday, will exercise its right to vote. I worked as chairman of the Commission of Inquiry on Haiti with my colleagues from Windsor-St. Clair, Papineau-Saint-Michel and Chicoutimi, and our friend Leo Duguay, who is no longer with us. I therefore want to wish Haiti good luck. I have visited the country and travelled there at least three times, and I know that to them it is extremely important. While we are discussing lowering the voting age from 18 to 16, they are anxious to exercise their franchise undisturbed, for once.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak to the motion presented by the hon. member for Kamloops concerning Bill C-332, whose purpose is to amend the Canada Elections Act.
Elections constitute the foundation of our political system and our democracy. It is the way we choose our governments and express the values that influence our public decision-making. That is why the right to vote is so important. I would first like to give a short history of the right to vote in Canada and then explain why the present voting age is 18.
In our first elections, which date back to the 18th century, the vote was limited to male property holders. From 1867 to 1920, the federal franchise was often manipulated in a blatantly partisan fashion by the political parties.
Until 1884, the federal franchise was based on provincial laws and included a property qualification, thus depriving large sections of the population of the right to vote.
During World War I, Canada adopted the War Time Elections Act and the Military Voters Act in 1917. These measures enfranchised members of the Canadian Armed Forces and their female relatives, while disenfranchising conscientious objectors and British subjects naturalized after 1902 who were bom in an enemy country or habitually spoke an enemy language. We have come a long way since then.
In 1918, women were first granted the right to vote federally.
In 1920, Parliament adopted legislation establishing the right to vote across the country and thus constituting the foundation of our present system. In 1948, the last statutory disenfranchisement of Asians was removed. The federal franchise was extended to the Inuit in 1950 and to status Indians in 1960.
It is now 1990. Canada has matured as a democracy and as a nation. Under our Constitution, Mr. Speaker, Canada now has a virtually universal franchise. All Canadian citizens 18 years of age and older are eligible to vote. The only exceptions are federal judges, inmates of prisons and mental institutions, and any person disqualified for corrupt or illegal electoral practices. These exceptions are specified in the Canada Elections Act.
Mr. Speaker, the present voting age is 18. It was lowered from 21 to 18 in 1970, and I think we should look at the reasons why changes were made at the time and see whether they put a new perspective on today's debate.
Voting rights for young people were a major legislative concern in many countries at the end of the 1960s.
In the Throne Speech on October 23, 1969, why the voting age was lowered. And I quote:
A disturbing element in many countries of the world has been the rising tide of unrest, particularly among young people. It has expressed itself in many ways, in public debate, in peaceful protest and sometimes in violence. Our profound disapproval of the excesses must not blind us to deeply felt and legitimate aspirations. Many citizens in our own country believe that they are entitled to assume greater responsability for the destiny of our society. Such demands, insofar as they do not

conflict with the general welfare, are the expression of a truly democratic ideal. They must be satisfied if our society is to attain its goals of peace and justice.
This was taken from the Throne Speech read on October 23, 1969.
A look at the debate on lowering the voting age as reported in Hansard shows that the proposal was very well received in the House of Commons. In 1970, it was felt that lowering the voting age from 21 to 18 was both appropriate and inevitable. This meant that 1,200,000 young people would have the right to vote.
At the time, it was felt that these were students who were well informed, interested and intelligent, and very much concerned about the problems and injustice of this world. Courses in civics, political science and related disciplines were becoming increasingly widespread.
Many people expressed the view that these young people would have a major impact on Canadian governments and their policies, an impact that would be very beneficial to the Parliament of Canada and the entire country.
There were other reasons for this initiative, Madam Speaker. First of all, it was the logical outcome of a process that had been going on for quite some time, especially since the last World War when 18 year-olds had been given technical and often dangerous jobs. Originally, the right to vote was very restricted, in one way or another, and for many years it was considered a privilege of the elite. The age of 21 was considered the age of maturity. In 1970, however, circumstances changed considerably. The decision to lower the voting age reflected a desire to channel the enthusiasm and energy of young people and get them interested in the country's politics, the theory being that out of boredom they might otherwise create a disturbance and get involved in reckless and often subversive activities.
Mr. Mazankowski was also very much in favour of lowering the voting age to 18. On November 3, 1969, at page 427 in Hansard he said:
We hear suggestions from our youth that political parties are irrelevant. They want more than mere participation at the polls at election time. They are looking for, a meaningful sense of participation. We in the various political parties all say that the
Private Members' Business
future of our parties depends on the involvement of youth. But what are we doing to encourage the youth of this country to become more active in political affairs? I hope possession of the franchise will instil in them a real sense of enthusiasm for the building of this country; God bless us, there is a great deal to be done. I am sure it will lead to much the same enthusiasm as many of us experienced in our election campaigns last year.
The feeling in 1970 was that by lowering the electoral age of majority, the government was attracting young people to the centres of decision.
Madam Speaker, at the time parliamentarians were almost unanimous in their support for lowering the voting age from 21 to 18. Most people felt that 18 year-olds were well educated, socially responsible and capable of making their own political decisions.
It is clear that the voting age was lowered for two main reasons: 18-year-olds were considered to be sufficiently mature to take part in our electoral system, and it was also clear that young people between the ages of 18 and 21 were demanding a bigger say in the government's decision-making process.
Personally, Madam Speaker, and these will be my final comments, I think 18 is the right age to have the right to vote.
I don't have the impression society has changed to the extent that we should give young people between the ages of 16 and 18 the right to vote. And I don't think young people under 18 are demanding the right to vote.
Madam Speaker, I think the Canada Elections Act should remain unchanged and should not be amended to set the voting age below 18.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a privilege to take part in the debate this afternoon. The previous speaker certainly made a major contribution to this debate. The hon. member for Kamloops who presented the bill expressed an idea that may be new but is nevertheless in the general interest. I am proud to support his bill and I also want to thank the hon. member for Cape Breton-Richmond East who seconded the motion for second reading of the bill presented by the hon. member for Kamloops.

As election reform critic for this party, I had the opportunity to appear before the Royal Commission on

Private Members' Business
Electoral Reform and Party Financing in connection with its study of the electoral laws of Canada.
In the course of our party's presentation, in which I was a participant before that Royal commission, I was asked a question about lowering the age to age 16. I believe the New Democratic Party had been before the commission just before and had proposed the idea embodied in the bill that has been introduced since by the hon. member for Kamloops. I was asked my opinion of it, and I gave my opinion then.
I will give it again to this House. I am not opposed to reducing the voting age. It just seemed to me there was not a hue and cry in Canada for a reduction in the voting age. If the consensus in the population is that we should leave the voting age at age 18 and not lower it, then I would go along with that.
I said that quite deliberately before the commission. I am repeating my own words because I know the hon. member for Kamloops was not there to hear them. He may find these new. In my view the Canada Elections Act is probably the most public act of any in Canada, except the Constitution of course. In so far as Canadians are concerned, it is the act they feel most close to in terms of interest in it and the way it applies to them. During the course of every election campaign thousands and thousands of Canadians become aware of some provision or another of the Elections Act. It touches our lives very directly. It may only be at specified intervals, every four or five years, but the fact is it does touch our lives at those times in a most direct way. Canadians have a very real interest in the Canada Elections Act and feel more possessive, I suggest, toward that act than almost any other that has been adopted or could be adopted in this Parliament.
For that reason, public input on this issue is vital. The royal commission is doing studies. The royal commission, I am sure, will be conducting some surveys in determining what Canadians feel about various aspects of the electoral law. I look forward to reading those surveys and to seeing the studies that are conducted by the commission before finally making up my mind on this issue. I believe this issue will be before Parliament, not just in the form of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Kamloops but in a comprehensive bill to amend the Canada Elections Act which I believe will be forthcoming from the Royal commission. At that time, if the
commission proposes a voting age of any number, I am sure that there will be a committee of this House studying the matter, returning to this House and asking us to approve or not the change in the voting age.
I hope that the hon. member for Kamloops, should this bill not have been passed by the time the Royal commission report comes to Parliament, would propose his amendment again at that stage so that we could discuss it and make a decision on it. It is important that the elected representatives of people make a decision, having heard the views of their constituents and of the public. I certainly would be interested in hearing those views. I would welcome correspondence on the issue at any time.
My impression-and I stress that it is an impression- is that there is not much clamour for a reduction of the age from 18 to any other age, be it 16, younger or older. There is general satisfaction with the age of 18 as is currently the case in the law.
I was interested to look back at the Debates when the voting age was lowered. When I was 18 years of age, I could not vote. I had to wait until I was 21, which dates me somewhat. I believe it was 1970 that the voting age was lowered to 18 from 21. There was a debate in this House about the act at that time. I ran across a quotation which was against lowering of the age, and it was a view that did not prevail. I want to quote it because it was a very distinguished member of Parliament who was a neighbour of mine. He was the member for Frontenac- Lennox-Addington. His successor in this House would be the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac-Lennox and Addington. Mr. Alkenbrack was the member at that time. He made a speech on this very subject. I would like to quote from his speech at page 7461 of Hansard for May 28, 1970:
I am opposed, however, to lowering the age limit to 18 for those who stand for public office. I do not agree we have to go that far to show our young people that we are with them and that we think it is time for them to become active in government. No man or woman who has just reached the age of 18 has had a chance to receive either a full education or an appreciable degree of practical experience.
I do not necessarily share the views of the hon. member who spoke, but it is obvious that the people of Canada, by and large, shared that view. I do not believe an 18 year-old has yet been elected to hold a position in this House, although we have had some fairly young

members, none have been that young. Although the age has been lowered-

The other thing that was interesting going back in that debate in 1970 was to find out why the age of majority was put where it was, at age 21 at that time. It has been lowered to age 18 since.
I came across an interesting quotation in the debate at page 7399 of Hansard on May 27, 1970. The member who was speaking quoted from Holdsworth's "History of English Law". The quotation is from that. It is not really from the Hansard of that date but the speaker on that occasion used it. I would like to read the short section:
In Roman law young people were divided, like Gaul, into three parts. First, there was infantia which was ultimately fixed as under 7 -it is perhaps ironical that it is this word whose descendant has come to be used in our law for everyone under 21 -
Of course, that has been changed by statute to 18.
Roman historians state that the barbarians reckoned their young were old enough to cany arms and be counted as grown up at 15. And 15 became the general age of majority in Britain and northern Europe during the ninth, tenth and eleventh centuries, though not specifically linked with fighting ability. But by the time of the Norman Conquest there was a change of emphasis. The role of the mounted knight became more and more important, the armour heavier and heavier and the horses more enormous as time went on. By the time of Magna Carta the age for those holding in knight service had been raised to 21 and there is strong authority for the view that this was directly linked

with the ability to hold up a heavy suit of armour and lift a lance or
sword at the same time.
Perhaps that is an explanation of how we got to 21. Perhaps hearing that explanation our legislators in 1970 decided that 18 was a more appropriate age. In any event, that is the age we now have.
The hon. member for Kamloops and the members of his party have evidently, in convention, voted to lower the age to 16.1 know this is party policy. I assume it was adopted at a convention.
The hon. member has introduced this bill. I am pleased to support it in principle at second reading in order to allow for the matter to be studied in committee in this House where I hope the committee could review the provisions, hear from the public, and ultimately recommend the bill back to the House or not, with or without changes. I am happy to assist in seeing that the bill go to committee. I believe it is one that should be studied and then, if we choose to deal with it in a different way at third reading, we can each make up our own mind, having heard the evidence and having looked at the views of the people of Canada who, I think, will have something to say on this important subject. Those are a few thoughts on the matter.
I should add one more caveat about the Royal commission. The hon. member for Kamloops has this bill to amend the Canada Elections Act before this House. I also have introduced a substantial bill to amend the Canada Elections Act in a more comprehensive way. I have urged the government to accede to a request to refer all of these bills to a committee for study so that we can make a significant number of amendments to the existing Canada Elections Act, in order to have it in shape for the next election.
I have stated before and I will state again my concern that the Royal commission is not going to report in time to allow this House to deal with its report and make the changes to the Canada Elections Act that are necessary, if we are to run another election properly in Canada. I believe that, notwithstanding the very good intention of the Royal commission we, in this House, need to take the Canada Elections Act very seriously, look at it in a serious way and effect changes to it on a prompt basis, if

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, every once in a while when Canadians have come to the conclusion that this place cannot get any more foolish, that this House of Commons cannot get any more silly, when no member anywhere in the Parliament of Canada can come up with a more ridiculous idea, along comes the member of the New Democratic Party and saves us all from that notion that there is no bottom.
What we have before us today is the proposal that we lower the voting age to 16. The argument put forward was that there are capable people at age 16 who know how to vote. I want to say to the hon. member for Kamloops: He is absolutely right.
But, having said that he is absolutely right, exactly the same argument can be made for 15 year-olds, 14 year-olds, 13 year-olds, 12 year-olds, and 10 year-olds. There are, here and there, though in diminishing numbers, people of lower and lower ages who have the capacity to make the intellectual judgments about the running of the country and who are every bit as capable as an adult. But I submit that is not the question. One of the roots of the question here is whether or not we have a right, in this society, to make arbitrary judgments. We make arbitrary judgments in many things. We make arbitrary judgments in respect of our driving patterns and our driving laws in this country.
If the NDP would admit for a moment that we should remove those, then we would take down the stop signs which, arbitrarily, tell people at an intersection that they have to stop, look both ways, and then proceed. It is absolutely arbitrary in North America and in much of Europe today that you drive on the right-hand side of
the road. We cannot justify that it is better to drive on the right-hand side of the road than the left-hand side.
So the question really comes to, why do we have a voting age that is defined in any process at all. I think most Canadians would start from the presumption that you have to, in a free and democratic society as is granted by the Charter of Rights but within the reason of democratic capacity to put some judgment to it, not allow everybody from birth to vote. That simply means that you would then have a situation where the adult in that family would bear more influence if they had more children because they would exercise their vote through their children.
When we come to these questions as to whether or not young people ought to be able to vote under a certain age, it seems to me that it is appropriate to ask the question: what was the first principle of Parliament? The first principle of Parliament, some 730 years ago, was to control the King's purse. From the first principle, it has remained the most important principle every since. The most important reason why we assemble here is to control the expenditures of Parliament. That is what Parliament is about. It is about controlling public expenditures. There is no principle more important than that.
The truth of the matter is, in today's society, persons age 16 by law are not supposed to be obtaining permanent work. Yes, they get part-time work and they will work in some places with some dominance such as McDonald's fast food outlets, but they are unable to enter into contract. It seems to me that, at an age where they cannot enter into marriage of their own judgment, cannot enter into contract, cannot take on permanent work, that it is not the kind of life experience that then allows them to come to Parliament or to vote in Parliament for the question of asking the process: "Should I or should I not be able to make a judgment vis-a-vis the question of the public accounts of Canada?"
This silly idea of lowering the age simply because we know some people who are capable begs the question as to how far down do we go. Like the hon. member for Kamloops, I too could name those people in equal numbers to him. I do not know where we would stop but
December 14, 1990

I know of 10 year-olds whose capacity to comprehend Parliament astounds me and for which I give them tremendous credit.
Is Canada better if we open up that process? Is there not also to be viewed a notion that democracy itself is to be so cherished and so privileged that there may well be a benefit from the waiting period and that we come to a level of maturity, understanding, experience, and economic relationships before we are able to exercise our right to vote and to influence our country?
Surely, it seems that if we lower-and for the same reasons that the hon. member for Kamloops said today, I could lower it another year next year-I do not know how low we could go, but I think we could go a long way down and still justify it on the same basis. Is this notion of the vote to have no criteria attached or no privilege? The best judgments might well come from those who have had to observe and experience for a while before exercising their franchise.
I might say, as an aside, if I were to give the hon. member for Kamloops an award-as the hon. member for Nickel Belt would do-for the most foolish idea of the year, the first runner-up would be the Reform Party who I would presume would want to have the voting age raised to age 65.
We talk about this arbitrariness in, for example, driving cars or consuming alcohol. In my province of Alberta, the legal age for the consumption of alcohol is 18. In the province we are in at this moment, Ontario, it is 19. Those are two arbitrary ages and they are different. We know that there are persons who probably could consume modest amounts of alcohol at younger ages without harm, and there are some of them at the age of 53 years, or some other age, who may not be able to consume alcohol, wherever they may be, or ought not, or should not, and never will be able to.
We make those arbitrary decisions in life. We make them about entering into contract.
There are persons who are 18 years of age who should not enter into contract. We say they can because they are 18. There is no other reason. They lose their shirt and everything. It may very well be that, if they had waited until the age 30, they would still have lost their shirts.
There are historical examples of people who entered into business when they were 14. E.B. Eddy, who started
Private Members' Business
across the river here, is one Canadian example. At 14 years of age he entered into the business world. Sir John A. Macdonald was a lawyer when he was 16 years of age. Nevertheless we take society as we see it in the broad overview.
I want to come to another aspect of this question which I think should cause us to pause and reflect. What is the value of youth? What is the value of being a child? Is there not to be a period in our lives when we are carefree, when we have fun, and when we can take life from the imagery and imagination of being youthful, doing those kinds of things ought to be set aside for the purpose of children. They ought not to bear the burden of the workplace. They ought not to bear the burden of raising incomes. They ought not to bear the burden of having to vote or run for public office.
I submit for all the arguments that the hon. member for Kamloops used today to have the voting age go down, the same argument would be just as valid for 15 and 14 year-olds, perhaps even for 12 or 10 years of age. But somewhere along that line we encroach on something more important. We encroach on childhood, young adolescence, and on that period where there ought to be a time for not bearing the burden of the adult world. I submit the development of a human body is as important to protect as is the extension of rights that they ought to vote.
Give children the chance to have time to play. They grow up too fast now. Physical relations are too soon now. Alcohol consumption is too soon now. Why go one step further to ask that they now bear the burden of public office when they can bear in just two years later at the next election. Eighteen years is not a long time to wait to be granted for life the chance to run for public office, to vote, and to take part.
No one is doubting their capacity or their ability. It simply is a better approach to say: "Let them be children as long as they might".

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this afternoon I would also like to speak to the important tonic raised by the hon. member for Kamloops. Of course, it sounds good to say we will set the voting age at 16 instead of 18.

Private Members' Business
I remember-it seems it was only yesterday-when we were eligible to vote at 21. Most members of this House will recall that they all voted for the first time at the age of 21.
In the 70s, the voting age was lowered to 18. I have noticed, and I am not saying this is due to the fact that the voting age was lowered to 18, that we have had a number of problems since then which I intend to address here. Since the 1970s, parents seem to have shown progressively less interest in their children.
We often hear people say: "You are 18 now, so pick up your things and go and live your own life". This may be due to the fact that at that age they are now considered to be adults. Before, we used to hear this when a young person turned 21. They use to say: "At 21 you can stand on your own two feet, so go out and live on your own". Now this is being said to 18 year-olds. And across Canada, we see all the problems that young people are having. I very much agree with what the previous speaker said: Why do we want to take away the right of our young people to be young? I think that at 16, young people want to be young. They do not want to have more responsibilities than they can handle. At 16 they want to enjoy their youth.
My son is 20, and when he was eligible to vote, at 18-his first time was in 1988-he told me: "I am proud to have this responsibility but I think it is a little too soon". He said: "I may be privileged in having parents who helped me over the years to find out about the history of my country". He didn't necessarily learn all this in school. We told him about the history of our country. In any case, he felt better prepared than some of the kids in his group. He often told me: "Dad, lots of kids at my school went to vote, and they didn't even know why they were voting or who they were voting for". They had not yet developed an interest in government. They didn't realize what being eligible to vote was all about. In fact, it is a major, fundamental responsibility.
When I look at the way parents react and how they perceive their relationship with their children, I wonder whether we should really encourage this trend so that soon, parents will be saying: You are 16? Good. You are eligible to vote, so you can leave home and stand on your own two feet. I am not so sure a 16-year-old would be
able to stand on his own two feet and make his way through life and support himself. That just isn't so. I never believed that and I still do not. I do not think we, as parliamentarians, have the right to take away from our youngsters the right to be young and to have time to mature and to develop their personality.
It seems the hon. member's proposal comes in response to demands made by young people. There are young people in my riding, 15 and 16 year-olds, who are extremely mature. But they are the minority. And where do we find these young people? In all political organizations across the country, whether they are NDP, Liberal or Conservative. They come and they start learning how democracy works. They learn to work within the electoral process in a riding. They gradually form an opinion on how a country should be administered and governed. But they get this opportunity at the age of 12,13,14,15 or 16. I agree that as they get more involved in the political process, they become increasingly anxious to vote. Well, they are eligible to vote at 18. People say: "Sure, but they can drive a car at 16".
I am still not convinced that letting a young man or a young girl of 16 get behind the wheel of an automobile is the best decision we could make in our lives. I am not sure that young people of that age are all very mature. I am not saying that they are all immature, but I am not convinced they all have the same level of maturity. Maybe 1 out of 100 or 10 out of 100 are mature enough to be allowed behind the wheel of an automobile. A car is just as dangerous as a firearm if you don't know how to use it. However, we cannot say yes to some and no to others. I am not convinced it was a very good idea to give them the right to drive at this age.
I remember that when the voting age was lowered to 18, people said that if they were old enough to vote, they were also old enough to have a pint in a tavern. So, naturally, the drinking age was also lowered from 21 to 18. I remember distinctly that I had my first beer in a public place at 21 years of age. If you were caught drinking under age then, you would get into serious trouble with the police, but mostly with your parents.
At 18, it's all right. You are capable of voting and you are capable of controlling your drinking. At 16,1 am not so sure people are mature enough to assess their drinking capacity and keep it within reasonable limits as we say. I am not convinced.

I have hardly a minute left, Madam Speaker, so I will conclude by saying that the idea is interesting and that many of our young people of 16 or 17 are indeed mature enough to vote wisely, but not to assume all the other responsibilities associated with that right. With a decision like this we, parliamentarians, would deprive a lot of our young people of two years of their youth, two years which they could enjoy freely without all these new responsibilities. The right to vote is the most important right given to an individual in Canada, and that right must be assumed.
I remember the first time I was told: "Mr. Ferland, you will be voting at such a place". When I entered the booth the first time to mark my ballot, I was quite nervous. It was a big responsibility. I did not spoil my ballot. I made my choice and I knew very well what the consequences were. Why impose such pressures on our young people? I think they have enough pressures as it is, in our society, without adding this new burden two years too soon.
